text:
INDIANAPOLIS – The low point wasn’t in the few days after Spencer Shrader’s right knee exploded.

There were no pity parties or “Why me?’’ reflections after Las Vegas’ Tristin McCollum dove into Shrader’s knee on a PAT attempt following Jonathan Taylor’s 3-yard run Oct. 5 at Lucas Oil Stadium. In the blink of an eye, the recently named AFC Special Teams Player of the Month of September was dealing with torn anterior cruciate and medial collateral ligaments in his business knee.

He was too preoccupied with simply walking again.

“The earliest days of rehab are the easiest because you’re just focused on one single goal, which is getting healthy and, like, walking again,’’ Shrader said Saturday at Lucas Oil Stadium. “There is no thought about, ‘Well, what am I going to kick like? What’s that process going to be like?’

“You’re focused on walking properly, then running properly, then being able to cut.’’

The low point that gnawed at Shrader’s confidence came during the early stages of training camp in Westfield when he still was trying to recapture his kicking mechanics. Too often, his field goal attempts drifted left.

“You have really high expectations for yourself,’’ he said. “I knew what I was capable of and not performing that way consistently – day after day during camp – just grinds you.

“Not to mention you’re in football for 12 hours a day, so I don’t get to do my normal things, which is hang out with my family and friends outside of football and go to my Bible studies, which keeps me fulfilled.’’

From a pure football standpoint, Shrader’s is a very good place.

Let the record show he’s walking – and kicking – just fine, thank you very much.

In the final duel for the Indianapolis Colts’ kicking job, Shrader likely ended the discussion by knocking down a 60-yard field goal in the third quarter of the otherwise inconsequential 25-16 loss to the Detroit Lions. It would have been good from 65, probably longer.

“I’ve hit 70 indoors before,’’ he said with a smile. “I’ve hit 70 in pregame at Lucas Oil. But everything has to go right for a 70-yarder.’’

Blake Grupe did nothing to tarnish his chances by converting 46- and 36-yarders, but the kicking job might have been Shrader’s to lose heading into the final preseason game.

“I think there’s a lot of appreciation, coming off an ACL, to be where he’s at,’’ coach Shane Steichen said. “To kick the 60-yarder today was huge. I’m really pleased with where he’s at.’’

Nothing’s official until Sunday at 6 p.m., but internally the Colts have expected Shrader to regain his form of last season and do enough to outkick Grupe. During those inconsistent early days at camp, they kept reminding themselves he tore two ligaments in his right knee 10 months prior.

So much goes into the competition/evaluation, but some kicks are more impactful.

“In-game kicks carry the most weight,’’ special teams coordinator Brian Mason said.

So, the bottom line after three preseason games:

Shrader was 5-for-5, connecting from 61, 60, 53, 48 and 46.

Grupe was 2-for-4, hitting from 46 and 36 against the Lions after missing a 61-yarder at New England and pushing a 36-yarder wide right against Atlanta.

Shrader admitted he seldom sleeps well the night before a game because of the looming anticipation and expectations. Often, a professional kicker’s place on the roster can be a week-to-week proposition.

“I definitely sleep better having that weight off of me,’’ Shrader said.

If he enjoyed a sound sleep Saturday night, it wasn’t because he was confident the 60-yard field goal clinched his roster spot.

“I still don’t know,’’ Shrader said. “You do everything you can to put yourself in a good position. At the end of the day, those decisions aren’t yours to make. For me as a man of faith, I just have to trust in God’s plan wherever He leads me.

“If it’s not playing for Indianapolis, I have to find a way to battle that and get into a mindset where, ‘OK, I’ve been called to another chapter.’ If it is here, I just need to do what I was able to do in the preseason games and do that same thing in the regular season.’’

The one thing Shrader won’t do is dwell too long on the 60-yard punctuation mark to his preseason.

“It counts internally,’’ he said. “It is confidence-inspiring. It gets you back in a place where you know you can do it.

“But the danger some guys get caught in is you can’t live in the past, whether it’s good or bad. Now, I can’t rely on that 60-yarder. Now, it’s about week 1 of the season, preparing myself to be able to do that again.

It’s a little bit of an exhausting mindset, but it’s also the challenge that comes with it. That’s your biggest challenge as an NFL kicker. Can you approach every single day and every single week like it’s a brand-new week and continue to perform at an elite level? It’s a difficult thing to do.

Injury update

Coleman Owen suffered a concussion on the third play of the game. The wideout sustained head trauma while being blasted out of bounds at the end of a 12-yard reception.

Owen is competing for a roster spot as a sixth receiver and/or returner.

Backup QB

For those keeping track, Anthony Richardson Sr. enjoyed a better first half than Riley Leonard in the battle to be Daniel Jones’ backup.

Richardson started and played into the second quarter, completing 7-of-10 passes for 80 yards while absorbing one sack. His first two possessions stalled and led to Grupe’s field goals.

Leonard took over in the second quarter and completed 3-of-7 passes for 48 yards and an interception. The interception was the product of Leonard being pressured and forcing a throw while backing up.

Richardson’s first completion was a 24-yard hookup with Keenan Allen.

“I just wanted to go out there and just operate the offense. Be confident,’’ he said. “I was out there with some of the starters, so I just wanted to go out there and just showcase that I could just manage the game and just be out there and let it rip.

“I think I did that to a certain extent, and I’m feeling pretty good about it.”

Team celebration

No sooner had running back DJ Giddens registered a 6-yard TD run in the second quarter than most of his teammates sprinted from the sideline to maximize the celebration.

It was a planned penalty for delay of game.

“I wanted those guys to have fun,’’ Steichen said. “I want to say, ‘Shoot, it’s our last preseason game. It’s the last time this group’s going to be together . . . bring energy and every time we score, go celebrate together.’’’

title: Taking a look at Nick Morris and the kids - Jim Sumner | Substack
description:
Still, CBS chose to fcous on a middle linebacker, wiring him up through practices and an exhibition game.

Which brings me to 2026 and Nick Morris.

Nick Morris is a very bright man.
text:
In 1960 CBS aired a show entitled “The Violent World of Sam Huff.” Sam Huff was the star linebacker of the New York Giants. The Giants had just lost the 1958 and 1959 NFL championship games to the Baltimore Colts, the former still regarded as the Greatest Game ever played.

But the Giant were in the media capital of the world and players like Frank Gifford were about as well known as anybody in the NFL universe. Still, CBS chose to fcous on a middle linebacker, wiring him up through practices and an exhibition game.

Walter Cronkite narrated the show.

Fun fact. Cronkite was the keynote speaker at my Duke graduation.

I miss Walter Cronkite.

Back to Huff. This show solidified the middle linebacker as the biggest, baddest, meanest dudes on the football field, all at a time when the NFL was passing major league baseball as the most popular sport in the United States.

Huff wasn’t alone. By the end of the decade Ray Nitschke, Tommy Nobis, Joe Schmidt and our own Mike Curtis became household names. The AFL gave us Nick Buoniconti, whose son Nick, Jr. played for Duke.

And of course, the baddest of them all, Dick Butkus and I say that as someone who has never been a big Bears fan.

Let me add that Jimmy Brown wasn’t a middle linebacker and he’s the best football player to ever put on shoulder pads and I’ll die on that hill.

Of course, I imprinted on this narrative and despite all the fun-and-gun, four wideouts, I still think linebackers should be mobile, hostile and agile, all while immediately dissecting an opposing offense and keeping interlopers off the field/

If you don’t get that final reference, research Mike Curtis. circa December 11, 1971.

Curtis isn’t the only truly great Duke linebacker. Bob Matheson was only a few years behind him at Duke and he had a distinguished 13-year NFL career.

Curtis (Baltimore) and Matheson (Miami) were key players on Super Bowl champs.

Since then Duke has had some notables at linebacker, Dick Biddle and Keith Stoneback and Carl McGee and Mike Junkin. More recently, Michael Tauiiliili, Vinnie Rey, Kelby Brown, Joe Giles-Harris and Ben Humphries.

I’m sure my keen-eyed readers will alert me to some omissions.

Not all of these guys were middle linebackers. It’s hard to have a middle linebacker if you’re running a 3-4 or 4-2-5 defense and Miami’s famous “53”defense was predicated on their ability to line Matheson up pretty much anywhere he was needed.

Which brings me to 2026 and Nick Morris. Linebacker might be Duke’s deepest and most talented position and Morris might be the Duke player easiest to root for.

Nick Morris is a Connecticut native but spent his final high-school season in Texas. He didn’t play at all as a true freshman in 2021 and only played six games in 2022.

But he broke out in 2023, starting the final five games of the season. He had 61 tackles that season, a sack and a fumble recovery.

Morris is 6-3, 240, fast and strong. He’s appeared on Bruce Feldman’s “Freaks list.”

But his knees didn’t get the memo. He didn’t make it out of the 2024 opener against Elon before suffering a season-ending right-knee injury.

Surgey, rehab, work and pain, all the usual stuff and Morris was back on the field for 2025.

This time he lasted four games before another ACL injury shut him down, first quarter against NC State.

One of those games was against Illinois. He had three tackles for loss against the Illini.

Nick Morris is a very bright man. He has been Academic All-ACC, Academic All-District. He graduated from Duke last spring with a degree in economics. It would have been easy for him to decide that his body had given him everything it had to give and maybe it was time to move on with the rest of his life.

Not a chance. Morris is back, a sixth-year, enrolled in Duke’s Fuqua School of Business, a graduate degree down the road.

Morris isn’t on the freaks list anymore. Now he’s on the Comeback Player of the Year Award Watch List.

Yes, that’s a thing.

Can he pull it off?

He says yes, emphatically.

text:
The NFL world collectively held its breath last week when Las Vegas Raiders running back Ashton Jeanty went down with an injury during practice.

Jeanty went down after diving for a catch and had to be helped off the field after a fall. He seems to have avoided a long-term injury, which allowed Raider Nation to exhale after a few hours.

We don't know much about when Jeanty will return to play, but he won't miss the entire season, which is good for the team and his development as a running back. In the meantime, the Raiders will see how valuable he is to this offense in his absence.

Let's explain.

Ashton Jeanty's Value

Jeanty's rookie season didn't go very well, despite totaling more than 1,300 scrimmage yards and scoring 10 touchdowns. He was constantly getting hit behind the line of scrimmage because of the team's poor offensive line, and he wasn't running the ball very efficiently.

However, that doesn't tell the full story of the football player Jeanty is and who he is going to become. The star rusher from Boise State is still in there somewhere, and this is the perfect coaching staff to unleash his talent.

Klint Kubiak helped the Seattle Seahawks win the Super Bowl because of how well the team ran the football and how efficiently the offensive line played, despite not having many household names up front. The situation he creates for Jeanty will be much more beneficial than the one he faced in 2025.

For starters, Kolton Miller is back healthy at left tackle, so the Raiders should be able to run the ball to that side. They also added much better, NFL-level linemen, like Tyler Linderbaum and Spencer Burford, on the interior.

Is Mike Washington Jr. Ready?

Rookie fourth-rounder Mike Washington Jr. has turned heads throughout the preseason because of his explosiveness, and he should be effective in a potentially elevated role.

Washington is explosive, no doubt, but he currently lacks what it takes to be an every-down back, lacking the rushing consistency to carry the workload efficiently. He may get there someday, but the Raiders need him to be a home run-hitting back off the bench.

Jeanty has a star element that not many backs in the NFL have. The Raiders won't be able to run the ball as well without him, and they'll see his impact when he's out -- and when he returns.

description:

text:
Keenan Allen makes his Indianapolis Colts debut: Some of the answers around how Allen will be used by the Colts were answered in this game.

The Colts have their backup running back: Seventh-round rookie Seth McGowan has started all three preseason games.

PFF's fantasy football recap focuses on player usage and stats, breaking down all the vital information you need to achieve fantasy success in 2026.

With fantasy drafts happening right now, now is the time to prepare. Build your rankings with the Fantasy Rankings Builder, practice with the Mock Draft Simulator, get real-time help from the Live Draft Assistant and dig into the Fantasy Draft Kit, Fantasy Rankings and PFF Premium Stats to make every pick with an edge.

Detroit Lions @ Indianapolis Colts

Keenan Allen makes his Colts debut: The former Los Angeles Chargers wide receiver played four of six snaps on the first drive.

The Colts lost Michael Pittman Jr. via trade, leaving Alec Pierce and Josh Downs as the top two wide receivers on the depth chart. They added Allen during training camp to be among the top three receivers. Both Downs and Allen have historically played in the slot, so one big question was who would suit up in the slot. The other wonder was how snaps would be distributed in two-receiver sets. Downs hasn’t typically played in two-receiver sets, but Allen also didn’t typically play in two-receiver sets last season. Neither Pierce nor Downs played in this game.

The first question appears to be answered, as Allen was consistently lining up out wide in this game, with Coleman Owen or Anthony Gould in the slot. The Colts could have easily used Laquon Treadwell and Ashton Dulin out wide and moved Allen to the slot, and that arguably would be the better lineup and their likely route if both Pierce and Downs are injured. This suggests that Allen will be a Z receiver this season, leaving Downs in the slot in 11 personnel. The Colts only ran one play out of 12 personnel on the first drive, and Allen was on the field, suggesting they are comfortable playing Allen in that personnel grouping. However, that doesn’t speak to how much he might play it over Downs. It was worth noting that Allen left the game for two plays after making a 24-yard catch, suggesting his playing time will be at least somewhat limited.

Further down the depth chart, it appears Treadwell is the backup X receiver, even though Ashton Dulin was the backup X at times last season. Pierce is returning from the PUP list, but might not be ready for Week 1. If Pierce can’t play in Week 1, Treadwell appears to be the starter. Dulin played with the starters, but only in place of Allen at Z. Both Treadwell and Dulin were done at this point, with Nick Westbrook-Ikhine and seventh-round rookie Deion Burks coming in after them. Owen played ahead of Gould in the competition for the backup slot role, but got injured on his second play.

Seth McGowan plays ahead of DJ Giddens: McGowan appears to be the current favorite for the backup job behind Jonathan Taylor.

Giddens was drafted in the fifth round of 2025 to be the Colts’ backup running back, but Indianapolis later decided to add Ameer Abdullah for that role. They didn’t re-sign Abdullah, but drafted Seth McGowan in the seventh round to compete with Giddens. Giddens missed the first two weeks of the preseason with a hamstring injury, allowing McGowan to start both matchups.

In this game, McGowan played every snap with the starters. He also played the first few snaps of the second drive with backups before Giddens took over. This suggests McGowan is currently ahead of Giddens. This would make McGowan the back to draft in deeper leagues where most handcuffs are selected. However, if Taylor suffers a serious injury, it wouldn’t be surprising if the Colts traded for a running back rather than relying on McGowan.

Lions compete for the backup wide receiver spots: A knee injury landed Cedrick Wilson Jr. on injured reserve, opening a roster spot for another receiver.

Amon-Ra St. Brown and Jameson Williams sit at the top of the Lions' wide receiver depth chart, and neither has played in the preseason. Isaac TeSlaa played a surprising amount over the first two preseason games, but was among the starters to sit in this showdown. Wilson had appeared locked into one of the backup spots, but now that he’s on injured reserve, he won’t be among the top backups.

Tom Kennedy is the next man up among the outside receivers, and appears to have secured a roster spot. He has played 30 games for the Lions over the last seven seasons, and he may be more involved this season than in the past. He is also competing to be a returner, and took the first punt return for Detroit in this game.

Greg Dortch appears to be the next man most likely to make the roster after only playing in the first half last week. He was playing in the slot in 11 personnel early in that game, but played longer than you would expect for someone who has a secure roster spot. Dortch is also in contention for the punt return job, but if Kennedy has won it, there is no guarantee Dortch makes the roster.

Tay Martin and Lucky Jackson were the other starters for this game, and there is a solid chance one of them will make the roster, although it’s also possible Detroit will sign someone who was released elsewhere instead of keeping one of these players.

Miscellaneous Notes

The Lions continued to sit quarterback Jared Goff, running back Jahmyr Gibbs, wide receivers Amon-Ra St. Brown, Jameson Williams and Isaac TeSlaa and tight ends Sam LaPorta, Brock Wright and Tyler Conklin.

Backup Isiah Pacheco remains out due to a back injury. It’s unclear whether Sione Vaki didn’t play because he is still injured, or if he was far enough up the depth chart.

The Colts rested quarterback Daniel Jones, running back Jonathan Taylor and wide receiver Josh Downs.

While Alec Pierce was activated off the PUP list earlier this week, he did not play in this game.

Tight end Tyler Warren missed this game with a groin injury. Drew Ogletree and Will Mallory also didn’t play due to injury.

Chicago Bears @ Tennessee Titans

Nicholas Singleton continues to play only on early downs: The Titans’ fifth-round pick consistently left the field for Michael Carter on third downs.

Tony Pollard and Tyjae Spears are currently locked into the top two spots on the depth chart. Tennessee drafted Singleton with 2027 in mind, as both Pollard and Spears are set to become free agents. However, if the Titans’ season doesn’t go as well as they hope, they could start looking toward the future at some point this season.

During the first week of the preseason, Singleton didn’t enter the game until late in the second quarter. He played into the third quarter, logging 16 snaps on first and second downs but only one on third down. Carter, meanwhile, played eight snaps on first and second downs and five on third down. Singleton missed last week due to injury but started this game. Tennessee used a similar rotation, with Carter consistently replacing Singleton on third downs.

Nearly every team uses its running backs in a variety of situations during the preseason, regardless of down and distance. The fact that the Titans aren’t using Singleton on third downs even in the preseason strongly suggests they have no intention of giving him that role during the regular season. If Singleton starts seeing playing time this season, it would therefore be more likely to come at Pollard’s expense than Spears’, as Pollard tends to play more on early downs while Spears handles more third-down work.

While Pollard didn’t play in this game, his usage in the first two preseason contests was concerning, as Spears out-snapped him with the starters in both. Pollard remains a risky fantasy option despite sitting atop the Titans’ depth chart.

Miscellaneous Notes

The Titans rested quarterbacks Cam Ward and Mitch Trubisky, running backs Tony Pollard and Tyjae Spears, wide receivers Calvin Ridley and Wan’Dale Robinson, and tight ends Gunnar Helm and Daniel Bellinger.

First-round rookie Carnell Tate started the game but played only the first drive.

K.J. Osborn has a shot to make the roster as Tennessee's sixth receiver. He played only in the second half of the first week of the preseason and didn’t play last week. In this game, he was Tate's primary replacement starting on the second drive.

The Bears rested quarterback Caleb Williams; running backs D’Andre Swift and Kyle Monangai; wide receivers Luther Burden III, Rome Odunze and Kalif Raymond; and tight ends Colston Loveland and Cole Kmet.

Jahdae Walker appears locked in to the Bears’ fifth wide receiver spot. Last week, his day was done at halftime, and everyone below him on the depth chart played into the fourth quarter. This week, he and third-round rookie Zavion Thomas were the starters. Walker played only the first quarter, while the other starters played the rest of the first half. Thomas is locked in to the fourth receiver spot.

Table Notes

Snaps include plays called back due to penalties, such as offensive holding or defensive pass interference. The other three stats have these plays removed.

Targets may differ from official NFL sources. The most likely discrepancy would be from a clear thrown-away pass, where the NFL may give the target to the nearest receiver, while this data will not.

text:
EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. (AP) — Chip Trayanum was taken to a hospital with a neck injury after earlier running for a touchdown in the New York Jets’ 23-6 preseason loss to the Giants on Friday night.

The Jets announced that Trayanum, an undrafted rookie running back from Toledo, was awake, alert and had movement in his extremities.

“I think he’ll be just fine,” coach Aaron Glenn said after the game. “He’ll be just fine.”

Trayanum saw extended snaps and finished with 38 yards on 12 carries as Glenn and the Giants’ John Harbaugh rested almost all of their projected starters. With 10 seconds remaining before halftime and with the ball deep in their own territory, the Jets opted to hand it off to Trayanum — who was immediately walloped by Trace Ford.

Jets players and coaches remained on the field — many on their knees and praying — as Trayanum was examined in a scary and eerily quiet scene at MetLife Stadium. He was put in a neck brace, strapped to a backboard and loaded onto a cart and driven off the field.

The 24-year-old native of Akron, Ohio, played a major role on offense early with the Jets (1-2).

After Marcelino McCrary-Ball intercepted Jameis Winston — who started in place of Jaxson Dart — on a pass intended for Odell Beckham Jr. that was deflected by Qwan’tez Stiggers, the Jets’ offense hit the ground running.

Literally.

The Jets ran on 10 straight plays, including nine by Trayanum, who capped the drive with 1-yard touchdown run. Rookie quarterback Cade Klubnik, starting in place of Geno Smith, had the other rush on a 6-yard scramble.

Jason Sanders, who won the Jets’ kicker competition this week by beating out Cade York, was wide left on the extra point. He also was short on a 54-yard field-goal attempt.

With the Giants (2-1) driving deep in Jets territory on their next possession, McCrary-Ball punched the ball out of Braxton Berrios’ hands and Stiggers recovered in the end zone for a touchback.

The Jets couldn’t take advantage and went three-and-out. A 16-yard run by Tyrone Tracy and a 23-yard catch by Beckham got the Giants to the 6, and Tracy ran it in to put the Giants up 7-6 with 28 seconds left in the opening quarter.

Klubnik has a so-so showing in his bid to be the Jets’ No. 2 QB

Klubnik, a fourth-round pick, was intercepted early in the second quarter by Zaire Barnes, a sixth-rounder of the Jets in 2023 who signed with the Giants last year. It was Klubnik’s first turnover of the preseason.

He played the entire first half and was 6 of 13 for 59 yards and the INT. He was replaced by Bailey Zappe to start the third quarter.

“Overall, not my best ball,” Klubnik said.

Glenn said Klubnik was “up and down” and declined to declare him the No. 2 quarterback behind Smith.

Beckham almost makes a sparkling play like the OBJ of old

Beckham, possibly looking to secure a roster spot, caught three passes for 53 yards on six targets in the first half. But he nearly had an amazing catch.

Early in the second quarter, Beckham got behind the coverage and Winston threw a deep pass that appeared on its way to being a 73-yard touchdown. But the ball was slightly overthrown and Beckham dived, but it went off his fingertips when he hit the ground.

“I don’t want to say exactly that he’s making it right now or not, what the considerations are, and things can happen,” Harbaugh said. “But I think I would answer the question, yes, I think he has done enough to make an NFL roster, for sure. He’s played well.”

The 33-year-old Beckham, a first-round pick of the Giants in 2014 who played five seasons with the franchise, re-signed with his original team in June. His chances of making the roster improved when Calvin Austin tore the ACL in his right knee earlier this week.

“Super grateful for the opportunity,” Beckham said. “At this point, it’s in God’s hands. I know that I have a good feeling about myself. I feel like there’s ball to be played, plays to be made.”

Haener leads late TD drive for Giants

Jake Haener, fourth on the Giants’ depth chart behind Dart, Winston and Brandon Allen, had a 37-yard touchdown pass to Xavier Gipson in the fourth quarter.

Haener, who spent his first three NFL seasons with New Orleans, signed with the Giants last week.

Zvada wins Giants’ kicking competition

Harbaugh announced that rookie Dominic Zvada won the Giants’ kicker job, beating out Ben Sauls.

Zvada kicked field goals of 23, 53 and 46 yards against the Jets and made both of his extra points.

Injuries

Giants: Tracy left in the second quarter to be evaluated for a concussion, but was cleared to return.

Jets: Glenn said CB Tre Brown was taken to a hospital because of a finger injury. ... Edge rusher Joseph Ossai left in the first quarter with a foot injury. ... Rookie G Anez Cooper, a sixth-round pick, was ruled out after injuring his right shoulder in the second quarter. ... WR Cam Camper was evaluated for a concussion in the second half and cleared. ... RB Dominic Richardson injured an elbow in the fourth quarter.

Up next

Giants: Host Dallas in a Sunday night matchup on Sept. 13.

Jets: Take on former coach Robert Saleh and the Titans in Tennessee on Sept. 13.

text:
Preseason NFL football is about to be behind us, and Week 1 of the fantasy football season is less than two weeks away. With only training camps and beat reporter news left to use, fantasy managers have to get a better handle on injury situations around the league and their potential implications for the 2026 season.

There are various injuries to monitor heading into the start of the season. Some of them have had massive updates in the last few days. Let’s take a look at some of the standout injury storylines we have been tracking.

Fantasy Football Research & Advice

Fantasy Football Expert Rankings

2026 Fantasy Football Draft Kit

Fantasy Football Trade Analyzer

Fantasy Football Injuries to Monitor

FantasyPros offers audio versions of articles using Instaread.

Ashton Jeanty (RB – LV) | Ankle

This is the biggest concern that popped up for fantasy managers this week. Ashton Jeanty suffered an ankle sprain in practice, and while the injury is reportedly not considered major, there is still a small chance he won’t be ready for Week 1.

That’s important because Jeanty is being drafted as a first- or second-round fantasy running back. The good news is that reports indicate it is a low-ankle sprain rather than a high-ankle sprain, but the lack of a firm return timeline makes him one of the most important players to monitor over the next two weeks.

Breece Hall (RB – NYJ) | Groin

Breece Hall suffered a groin strain earlier this month and was initially expected to miss 2-3 weeks. The encouraging part is that the Jets and their trainers continue to believe he’ll be ready for Week 1.

Still, groin injuries can be particularly troublesome for running backs because they impact acceleration and explosiveness and can tend to recur. Hall’s absence has given Braelon Allen and Isaiah Davis additional opportunities in camp, but the Jets want Hall to be a bell-cow back this season.

Puka Nacua (WR – LAR) | Groin

Puka Nacua’s injury is less concerning than Ashton Jeanty’s or Breece Hall’s, but his fantasy value makes it worth monitoring. He has been dealing with groin soreness and has missed practice, although the Rams reportedly expect him to be ready for Week 1.

The issue at this point in the first round is opportunity cost. Nacua is being drafted among the elite fantasy receivers, so there’s a meaningful difference between taking him at his current average draft position (ADP) and taking him after another elite receiver such as Ja’Marr Chase or Jaxon Smith-Njigba.

With Nacua, there is also a small chance of a short suspension, but that diminishes with each passing day.

Malik Nabers (WR – NYG) | Knee

Malik Nabers has an injury that dates back to last season. He’s returning from an ACL and meniscus injury and has had a complicated rehabilitation process over the last few months. The good news is that Giants head coach John Harbaugh recently said it is “reasonable to assume” Nabers could be ready for Week 1, and Nabers has been practicing without a non-contact jersey.

That makes Nabers one of the most interesting players in fantasy drafts. His talent is obvious, but you’re essentially betting on how quickly he’ll regain his pre-injury explosiveness. If he is available in the fourth round of drafts, I’m jumping on him at that cost.

Tyler Warren (TE – IND) | Groin

Tyler Warren’s groin injury isn’t currently believed to be serious, but it’s worth watching because he’s coming off an excellent rookie season and is being drafted as a top-four tight end. The Colts initially indicated he could miss roughly a week, but he has continued to be limited.

The biggest question isn’t necessarily whether he’ll play in Week 1. It’s whether he’ll have enough practice time to enter the season at full strength. With Alec Pierce off the physically unable to perform (PUP) list and Keenan Allen now on board, there is also more target competition.

Emeka Egbuka (WR – TB) | Toe

Second-year wide receiver Emeka Egbuka suffered a toe sprain during joint practices and has now missed close to two weeks. The injury was initially described as stable and not expected to jeopardize Week 1, but he still hasn’t returned to team drills.

That’s worth monitoring because Egbuka is expected to be a major part of Tampa Bay’s passing game without Mike Evans. Toe injuries can also be particularly annoying for receivers, so pay close attention here.

George Kittle (TE – SF) | Achilles

George Kittle is one of the most important injury situations to monitor because he is attempting an aggressive return from a torn Achilles suffered in January. The good news is that he has cleared a major hurdle. San Francisco activated him from the PUP list on August 23rd, making him eligible to play immediately rather than requiring him to miss the first four games.

Kittle has also returned to practice, although his initial work was limited to individual drills rather than full team activity. He is now just over seven months removed from the injury, which would make a Week 1 return an unusually quick recovery for an Achilles tear. But at this point, we can expect him to play in the league’s opening match in Australia.

TreVeyon Henderson (RB – NE) | Ankle

TreVeyon Henderson suffered an ankle injury that has been an issue in practice, but the latest reports are encouraging. He’s now expected to be good to go for Week 1.

Henderson is one of the more popular breakout candidates in fantasy drafts. Even a relatively minor ankle problem can be significant for a running back whose fantasy appeal is heavily tied to explosiveness.

Josh Jacobs (RB – GB) | Groin

Josh Jacobs has been dealing with a groin injury since early August and has missed preseason action. Green Bay has remained optimistic about his recovery, but he hasn’t been able to return to the field consistently.

This is relevant because Jacobs is coming off a huge fantasy season and should once again have a substantial workload. We do have the legal issues with Jacobs resurfacing again this week, so a suspension could be on the horizon. But fantasy managers shouldn’t expect his health to keep him out of games, at least initially.

Jordyn Tyson (WR – NO) | Hamstring

Jordyn Tyson is one of the more serious concerns on this list, as he has had chronic hamstring problems. The rookie receiver suffered a hamstring injury that was initially expected to cost him around two months, meaning he won’t return until sometime in October.

That’s a major problem for a player who was generating significant fantasy sleeper buzz. But no matter how talented he is, if Tyson can’t figure out how to stop the hamstring from getting injured, none of it will matter.

Tucker Kraft (TE – GB) | Knee

Tucker Kraft’s situation has become considerably more encouraging over the past couple of weeks. He tore his ACL in Week 9 last season after an incredible start, posting 32 catches for 489 yards and six touchdowns in just eight games. He has been working his way back throughout training camp and recently progressed to 11-on-11 work.

The latest news is good: Kraft participated in 11-on-11 drills during Green Bay’s joint practice with Arizona and is now expected to be a full participant in Week 1. That represents a change from earlier in camp, when the Packers limited his reps for much of the start of camp after he was allowed to practice.

Alec Pierce (WR – IND) | Ankle

Alec Pierce moved in the right direction on Thursday, as Indianapolis activated him from the PUP list after offseason ankle surgery. The Colts expect his workload to increase gradually and are hopeful he’ll be ready for the opener.

Pierce still has to demonstrate that he can handle a normal NFL workload and that the ankle that has bothered him for some time won’t limit his long, explosive plays that got him a big contract this offseason.

Luther Burden III (WR – CHI) | Groin

Luther Burden III’s injury situation has taken a positive turn, but there is still enough uncertainty that fantasy managers should keep monitoring him. The second-year receiver suffered a groin injury on August 8th and was initially expected to miss roughly a month, which ruled him out for the preseason.

The encouraging development came this Wednesday, when Burden returned to practice for the first time since the injury. He was limited to individual drills and did not participate once the Bears moved into 7-on-7 work, so he’s not quite back to full speed yet.

Burden also participated in Thursday’s joint practice with Tennessee, so he is moving in the right direction. The Bears are optimistic he will be ready for the team’s season opener against Carolina.

NASHVILLE, Tenn. -- Tyson Bagent connected with Zavion Thomas for a 97-yard touchdown on Chicago's first offensive play and the Bears wrapped up the preseason Saturday night with a 24-15 win over the Tennessee Titans in a battle of mostly backups.

With Caleb Williams watching from the sideline, Bagent completed his first seven passes for 155 yards. He also tossed a 2-yard TD pass to Maurice Alexander in the second quarter, helping Chicago (2-1) convert its first four fourth downs.

ABC7 Chicago is now streaming 24/7. Click here to watch

Coach Robert Saleh had talked of building reps for his starters through the preseason games for his Titans (2-1). After a joint practice against each preseason opponent, all NFC playoff teams, Saleh started essentially backups with Cam Ward watching Will Levis start in a final display before the NFL cut deadline Sunday.

Bagent, undrafted out of Division II, showed again why the Bears signed him to a two-year extension in August 2025 to back up Williams. Bagent was 16 of 17 for 208 yards with two TDs before leaving with a 14-9 halftime lead.

Tennessee did start a trio of defensive regulars in end Jacob Martin, linebacker Cedric Gray and nickel cornerback Marcus Harris. Bagent had no problem beating the rest of the Titans' backup secondary featuring Keydrain Calligan and Micah Robinson.

Martin recovered a fumble credited to Bagent off a botched handoff on the second drive, prompting a celebration joined by All-Pro tackle Jeffery Simmons, end Jermaine Johnson II and rookie end Keldric Faulk who watched from the sideline.

Levis was 14 of 22 for 143 yards with a fumble he recovered off a botched handoff. The 33rd overall pick in the 2023 draft did lead the Titans to a trio of field goals, the last as time expired.

Bears and Titans use quarterback rotations

Case Keenum took over in the third quarter for Chicago. Roschon Johnson ran for a 3-yard TD with Cairo Santos adding a field goal to pad the lead to 24-9. Rookie QB Miller Moss, undrafted out of Louisville, played the fourth quarter for Chicago.

Hendon Hooker took over for Levis after halftime. Mitch Trubisky, signed in March to back up Ward, stayed on the sideline along with the Titans' starting quarterback.

Tennessee's lone TD came on a 9-yard run by D'Ernest Johnson with 3:50 left. The 2-point conversion failed.

Slye was the Titans' best offensive threat this preseason

Slye finished the preseason with 11 field goals, including becoming the first NFL player since the start of the 2017 preseason to make at least four in consecutive exhibitions. He added two more in the first half against the Bears and finished by making all five from 50 yards out or longer.

By halftime, he had 11 field goals for the most by any player in a preseason since Graham Gano had 13 in 2016 for Carolina.

Up next

Bears: Open the season Sept. 13 at Carolina.

Titans: Host Saleh's old team the New York Jets on Sept. 13.

text:
Roster cuts are already underway around the NFL, but the first reported New Orleans Saints decision was an easy call to make. NewOrleans.Football's Mike Triplett reports that injured wide receiver Mason Tipton will remain on the physically unable to perform list (PUP) when the regular season starts, giving him an opportunity to return later this year. That's because he started training camp on PUP.

Tipton, 26 in September, signed with the Saints as a rookie free agent out of Yale in 2024 and has caught 25 passes for 175 yards in his first 25 career games. He suffered a groin injury late last season and missed the final two games; the Saints put him on injured reserve just before the Week 18 finale with the Atlanta Falcons. It looked like a procedural move at the time to open a roster spot with so many injured players out of the lineup, but then he was held out of OTAs and minicamp during the spring. He still couldn't get on the field when training camp kicked off this summer, too, though he was seen working out off to the side with members of the training staff here and there.

So how does PUP work? Tipton will not count against the 53-man roster limit while on the list, and he can begin practicing as soon as Week 2, but he can't be activated for a game until Week 5. The soonest we could see him is Oct. 11's home game with the Minnesota Vikings. But it really depends on the severity of his injury. What's important is that the Saints have the option to bring him back when he's healthy.

What's the vision for him? Tipton was losing snaps to Rashid Shaheed and Brandin Cooks last year until the Saints moved on from both wideouts, and their offseason additions like Jordyn Tyson, Bryce Lance, and Barion Brown probably pushed him back down the depth chart. It's possible Tipton could find a role with Tyson sidelined by a hamstring injury, but if their recovery timelines are too close there may not be enough snaps to go around. It's a problem to solve another day.

The Minnesota Vikings QB2 battle has been between Carson Wentz and J.J. McCarthy. Furthermore, it appears that Wentz won that competition, but should he have? At least one former NFL player believes that neither of these two players should back up Kyler Murray.

Minnesota wrapped up its preseason with a 34-6 loss to the Denver Broncos on Aug. 28 at Empower Field at Mile High. Wentz made a brief appearance while an injury kept McCarthy out of this game.

Advertisement

Nonetheless, former NFL tight end Shannon Sharpe believes Max Brosmer outplayed Wentz and McCarthy this preseason. Sharpe also questions the availability of the veteran and the former first-round pick, both of whom have an injury history.

"Brosmer has outplayed [McCarthy]," Sharpe said on the Aug. 28 edition of "Nightcap." "All things being equal, they might keep him because of his youth, but I'm not trusting him. But it's really hard because Wentz hasn't been a picture of health. He's been injured a lot himself. He got injured in Philly [and] got injured in Indy; he's been injured damn near everywhere he's been. But I still trust him in a game that means something and you have to win more so than I trust J.J. McCarthy.

"I think Brosmer has outplayed both of them, to be honest with you guys. So if it was me, I would have Kyler as one, Brosmer as two, and then it's a toss-up for three. All things being equal, I think I would trade J.J. McCarthy and try to get draft compensation in the 2027 draft."

DENVER -- There was a bit of relief in Broncos coach Sean Payton's voice Friday night when he said wide receiver Marvin Mims Jr.'s right foot injury was not serious.

Mims left the preseason finale against Minnesota on Denver's first possession after he collided with a Vikings defender.

Mims was one of the few regulars Payton played in the game, so him going to the injury tent just a few snaps into a preseason game was not what the Broncos wanted to see.

"With Mims, he's going to be fine; it's a bruise," Payton said after Denver's 34-6 win. "So we were really more just cautious with him. There were a few guys that we were going to get some snaps with, certainly front-line guys for us, and he was one of those players."

Mims, a two-time Pro Bowl selection and first-team All-Pro as a returner in 2024, was one of the few Broncos regulars in uniform Friday. The fourth-year veteran was injured on an overthrown pass from quarterback Jarrett Stidham on the sixth play from scrimmage.

Mims and Vikings safety Jacob Thomas collided out of bounds as the ball sailed past the wide receiver, who immediately grabbed his right foot when he hit the ground.

An emotional Mims limped away and then tried to jog off the field before going to the injury tent. He then went to the locker room.

Mims, who is in the final year of his rookie deal, had missed several training camp practices because of a lower-body injury and did not have a catch or a return in the preseason.

He finished second in the NFL in punt returns last season at 15.6 yards per attempt.

The Broncos had 30 players who were not in uniform for Friday's game, including most of the team's starters.

text:
A vested player is one who has been credited with four or more seasons of NFL experience. To be credited for an NFL season, a player must have been on the active, inactive, IR, or PUP roster for three or more regular-season or postseason games. A player can also be credited for a season if they receive an injury settlement or grievance for the equivalent of three or more regular-season games. Note that a credited season is different from accrued seasons, which determine what type of free agent a player is.

Vested players do not go onto waivers and are free to sign with any team at any time, between the day after the Super Bowl and the NFL trade deadline. They are subject to waivers in the period after the deadline through the Super Bowl.

Non-vested players, or players with three or fewer credited seasons, are subject to waivers. If these players go unclaimed, they are free to negotiate with teams as free agents.

text:
The Dolphins face looming decisions with several injured young players, as they approach Sunday’s 6 p.m. deadline to reduce the roster from 90 to 53.

Defensive lineman Kenneth Grant remains “week to week” with an undisclosed injury, and the Dolphins have discussed the possibility of placing him on injured reserve with a designation to return as early as Week 5. But that decision has not yet been made, coach Jeff Hafley said Saturday.

Rookie tight end Will Kacmarek also is “week to week” with an undisclosed injury, Hafley said. He could become be an IR option, but that remains to be seen.

Quarterback Quinn Ewers was traded to Jacksonville for a 2028 sixth-round pick; he otherwise would have been an option for IR.

Teams can place two players on IR on Sunday as they cut to 53, essentially giving franchises 55 roster spots. Those two players who are moved to IR on Sunday can return after four weeks or anytime after that.

One of those two slots is expected to be used on linebacker Trey Moore, leaving the Dolphins with one slot to use on Grant, Kacmarek or anyone else with an injury.

“We have a bunch of guys still not ready to practice,” Hafley said. “I’ve got to make sure that we’re healthy.”

Those two players who could be placed on IR on Sunday automatically are designated to return and are eligible to play beginning in Week 5; teams can bring as many as eight players off IR in a season, and Sunday’s IR designations would count as two of them, whether the players return this season or not.

Hafley addressed other issues on Saturday:

▪ He said the team expects to keep two quarterbacks on the 53-man roster. Malik Willis will be one; a decision on the other looms among Ewers, Cam Miller, or (less likely) Mark Gronowski, or any quarterback who will be waived in the next few days.

▪ Theo Wease Jr. was released after dropping a touchdown catch during Friday’s preseason game. While not discussing Wease or any player specifically, Hafley said a player would not be released because of a single play.

▪ Dolphins starters ended up playing less than a quarter in preseason and not at all on Friday.

“In a perfect world, I would have loved starters playing into the second quarter” against Atlanta “but that just wasn’t best for where we’re at right now as a team” because of injuries and also because of the need to evaluate bubble players.

Hafley said a “lot of our ones got 40 plus reps” in joint practices with Washington and the Giants.

▪ Asked about the team’s depth, Hafley said the team is still “thin. We’ve got to develop the depth of the team. We’ve got to keep working with these guys. We’ve got to coach them better. We’ve got to develop these players to create more depth as we go.”

▪ In explaining his approach his preseason approach, Hafley said “we have three new systems on offense, defense and special teams. These are the infancy stages.”

He said the Dolphins were a “lot more scheme oriented” in practices than preseason games so that players could be clear-headed and not overthink as they made their case for roster spots during preseason games.

▪ The Dolphins have 3 1/2 practices this week and will begin game planning for their Sept. 13 opener at the Raiders.

▪ Here’s a look at the 13 players released by the Dolphins on Saturday. Please keep checking back here for updates on cuts.

Tagovailoa on return, boos

Falcons and former Dolphins quarterback Tua Tagovailoa, who was greeted with boos during Friday’s preseason game, lingered on the field afterward to embrace several former teammates and Dolphins staffers.

He was gracious in comments afterward.

“Being able to come back here, like, I’ve had six years here, and those are probably some of the best six years of my life,” he said.

“I had a Pro Bowl here, had a good amount of accolades. So, regardless of the reaction, I love the city. We have a home out here. It was really cool to see a lot of the guys after the game, and talk to some of the guys during the game. So it was a cool homecoming.”

Of the boos, he said: “It is what it is.”

Tagovailoa -- who fumbled a snap but completed 7 of 8 passes for 95 yards against backups during Friday’s 17-12 Falcons win -- said he understood the Dolphins’ decision to move on from him and spoke favorably of Hafley and general manager Jon-Eric Sullivan.

“I wasn’t playing up to the standard that I’ve been playing in years past, so I understand,” he said. “You’ve got to be real with yourself. I think Haf and Sully, they were really, really good in that process with me.

“We had a lot of conversations... And just the way they handled it I thought it was very professional. So kudos to them and got a lot of respect for them.”

text:
NFL

Patrick Mahomes' status for Chiefs' season opener revealed

Patrick Mahomes suffered a complex knee injury late in the 2025 season. However, unlike most players returning from an ACL injury, the former MVP is expected to take the field for the season opener. No. 15 didn't suit up for the Kansas City Chiefs' preseason games, but he's been practicing without any limitations. That's why, according to NFL Network insider Ian Rapoport, the Chiefs fully expect him to be under center to face the Denver Broncos. Patrick Mahomes is on track to play in Week 1 “In my understanding, Patrick Mahomes is on track to start Week 1, which, if you followed closely, the kind of training camp that he has had, this is no surprise,” Rapoport said. “He was out there on Day 1, and he has hit every check mark, and by all accounts has looked as good on the field as really as he has had in several years. My understanding is he's had a better and more efficient training camp than really he has had in some time.” Of course, this can all change, but with enough time to prepare for the season opener, the former Super Bowl champion should be on track to take the field. The Chiefs might not have his best sidekick, though. Left tackle Josh Simmons is dealing with a back injury, and head coach Andy Reid hinted that he might need some time. Mahomes has looked as sharp as ever in training camp, but he'll go against one of the sturdiest, hardest-hitting defensive fronts in the season opener. Barring a setback, he won't shy away from that challenge.

NFL

Giants' John Harbaugh reacts to concerning Cam Skattebo report

A Wednesday report revealed that second-year New York Giants running back Cam Skattebo got into a bit of a skirmish with defensive backs Jevon Holland and Greg Newsome II when Skattebo "slid down after a reception and came dangerously close to taking out a couple of Giants DBs' legs." While Pat Leonard of the New York Daily News later claimed that Skattebo's "act is getting old to his defensive teammates," Connor Hughes of SNY insisted it "wasn't a serious fight" and wasn't "anything really to write home about." Per Josh Alper of Pro Football Talk, Skattebo was ultimately spotted "talking to his teammates in an attempt to smooth things over." Following practice, first-year Giants head coach John Harbaugh addressed the potential controversy. John Harbaugh: Cam Skattebo can be "infectious" in both a good and bad way "Skatt’s great," Harbaugh said. "He does bring a lot of energy. But he did get a 15-yard penalty at the end of practice. Did you notice that? That’s not infectious. Well, it is infectious, actually. Infectious in a bad way, right? Like infectious disease type of thing. We don’t want that. So, we want it to be directed in a positive way." During his rookie season, Skattebo's "infectious" personality made him a favorite among teammates and Giants fans. However, that campaign ended when he suffered a gruesome dislocation of his right ankle on Oct. 26, 2025. By all accounts, Skattebo is on track to be good to go for the Giants' regular-season opener against the rival Dallas Cowboys on Sept. 13. While Harbaugh likely wouldn't mind if Skattebo antagonizes Dallas players during that "Sunday Night Football" matchup, the coach understandably doesn't want any of his players committing 15-yard penalties. Giants player pours cold water over possible Cam Skattebo controversy On Wednesday, Giants offensive tackle Jermaine Eluemunor took to X and ripped Leonard for creating "a BS Narrative" regarding the Skattebo story. Fights among teammates are common during the final days of training camp, when everybody involved just wants to get to the regular season, but the Skattebo situation could be something to monitor over the next several months.

NFL

Latest report throws a bucket of cold water on Packers’ most desirable trade option ahead of the regular season

Green Bay hasn’t had serious conversations with the Arizona Cardinals in regards to Josh Sweat, and it seems like Brian Gutekunst won’t go after the edge rusher. The Green Bay Packers are not trading for Arizona Cardinals edge defender Josh Sweat ahead of the 2026 regular season. That much is clear after The Athletic’s Matt Schneidman reported that Green Bay has had zero contact with Arizona regarding Sweat, and general manager Brian Gutekunst has no plans to pursue that type of deal. “Based on what I heard earlier this week, I can confidently say that Josh Swett is not going to be a Packer”, Schneidman said on the podcast ‘Green Bay Beat.’ “Not now, not ever. Brian Gutekunst has not had a single conversation with the Arizona Cardinals about Josh Sweat. And I can say that confidently based on what I’ve been told.” The Packers would presumably benefit from adding a proven pass rusher to complement their edge defender group, especially early in the season with Micah Parsons still recovering from an ACL injury and expected to miss the first few games. But Green Bay does not appear interested in paying the price required to make it happen. Why cost and timing make the trade unrealistic Acquiring Sweat would demand significant compensation on two fronts: draft capital and salary. The Cardinals would likely require a mid-round or even high draft pick in return. On top of that, Sweat is slated to make $18.1 million in each of the next three seasons. The Packers’ actual cash obligation in 2026 would be $10.88 million because Arizona already paid his $7.22 million option bonus back in March, but the cap hit remains substantial. Even with limited guarantees beyond this season (only $3 million of the 2027 salary is guaranteed for injury), the Packers view the combination of draft pick cost and contract commitment for a 29-year-old player as a poor investment. That calculus fits the Gutekunst philosophy of prioritizing draft and development over expensive veteran acquisitions. Green Bay comfortable with current rotation The Packers seem content with the players they already have to fill the early-season void while Parsons works his way back. Lukas Van Ness, Barryn Sorrell, Brenton Cox, Dani Dennis-Sutton, and Collin Oliver form the rotation along the edge. Sweat would represent a short-term upgrade over that group, but the front office is unwilling to invest the necessary capital in both draft picks and contract dollars to make that move. Reporting out of Arizona indicates the Cardinals are not willing to trade Sweat at this point either. They want to compete early in the season. If things go south for the Cardinals, Sweat could potentially become available closer to the trade deadline around the middle of the season. By that point, however, Parsons should be back and healthy, which would eliminate the Packers’ primary reason for pursuing an edge rusher in the first place. Sweat does have a strong connection with Packers defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon from their shared time both in Philadelphia and Arizona, which fueled speculation about a potential reunion. But a personal connection alone does not override the roster-building principles that have defined Green Bay’s approach under Gutekunst. The Packers are keeping what they have, and Sweat will stay in Arizona for now.

MLB

Yankees Turn Heads With Surprising Anthony Volpe Announcement

The New York Yankees’ Triple-A club made a quiet but notable lineup decision on Saturday that immediately caught the attention of fans following the organization. While the major-league team prepared for a doubleheader against the Boston Red Sox at Yankee Stadium, the Scranton/Wilkes-Barre RailRiders posted their starting nine for a game against Worcester. Anthony Volpe was listed at third base and slotted second in the batting order. The assignment stood out because Volpe has spent nearly his entire professional career at shortstop and has played some second base in the minors. According to prospect observers, this marked only his fourth appearance at the hot corner and his first there since a Single-A game with Tampa on June 3, 2021. The experiment arrives after the 2019 first-round pick was optioned to Triple-A following a stretch in which he hit .240 with 41 hits, one home run, 19 RBIs, 20 runs and seven stolen bases across 56 major-league games this season. Social-media reaction mixed curiosity with skepticism. Some posters wondered whether the move signaled a longer-term effort to add versatility, perhaps with an eye toward the infield mix in the Bronx. Others questioned whether Volpe’s arm strength would play comfortably at third and suggested he would be better served taking regular work at second base. A few simply registered surprise that the familiar shortstop was suddenly listed at a new position. The timing of the experiment coincides with a Yankees club that sits 76-59 after 135 games, four and a half games behind the Tampa Bay Rays in the American League East. The parent club split the first game of Saturday’s doubleheader, falling 6-0 to Boston and leaving the series tied. Down on the farm, the RailRiders’ decision to give Volpe a look at third base looks like an attempt to expand his defensive profile while he works on his offensive consistency. Volpe has remained with the Yankees organization for all four of his professional seasons since being selected in the first round of the 2019 draft. The organization has long valued his athleticism and baseball instincts; giving him even limited exposure at a new position is consistent with the way many clubs now develop infielders who may need to slide around the diamond as needs arise. Whether the appearance becomes a one-off or the start of a more regular rotation remains to be seen, but Saturday’s lineup card made clear the Yankees are willing to test the idea. For now the story is straightforward: a well-known prospect is getting a rare look at third base in Triple-A on the same afternoon the big-league club is locked in a rivalry series. The results of that experiment, both in the field and at the plate, will be watched closely by those tracking how the Yankees intend to construct their infield over the final weeks of the season.

title: 49ers face NFL's toughest roster decisions ahead of Australia opener

text:
All NFL 53-man rosters must be determined by 6:00 pm EST on Sunday. All general managers and head coaches will face difficult decisions.

General manager John Lynch and head coach Kyle Shanahan are in the toughest position of all.

That is due to two factors. While all teams play their first games at roughly the same time, the 49ers play theirs the second earliest, on September 10, three days before the main slate. Why is that any more difficult than the Patriots and Seahawks, who play on September 9?

Because the 49ers play in Australia and will be leaving for Down Under on September 2. That is only two days after final cutdowns, and no practices are allowed for three days after the final preseason game.. John Lynch will only have a few days to decide whether to sign any players released by other teams. And, to that end, he and Shanahan will have to project which currently-injured players should be kept and who should receive an injury designation.

There are only two designations the team can use to "save" a player from the 53-man roster. One is the PUP list, but to be eligible, a player must have missed the entirety of training camp. That is why Mykell Williams will be placed on it.

The IR-designated to return list can be used on any player injured during training camp, but the team is allowed only two.

In both instances, the player must sit out a minimum of the first four games of the season.

Here is the conundrum at certain positions.

Offensive line

Heading into training camp, Shanahan and Lynch said the left guard position was an open competition.

The main contenders were Robert Jones, Connor Colby, and Carver Willis. Jones is currently out with an injury, and a time frame has not been given. The Niners tried Austen Pleasants at left guard, though he has mostly played tackle. Early on in that experiment, Pleasants got hurt. While it is supposedly not a serious injury, the timeline adds pressure to the decision.

At center, the initial depth chart had Brett Toth backing up starter Jake Brendel, with Drake Nugent the third stringer. Toth is currently out with a concussion.

On the outside of the offensive line, Vederian Lowe was the likely swing tackle, but he has missed camp with a high ankle sprain. Pleasants and Enrique Cruz are the other backups, but the more experienced Pleasants is hurt.

Are any of those injured linemen—two guards, two tackles, and a center—close enough to returning that they should be kept outright? Are they so far away they should be on the IR list? All have played in at least one practice. (I am not sure if Lowe's partial first practice makes him ineligible for the PUP list.)

How big is the risk of losing a player to another team if he is waived? There are some here who would be attractive backups to other organizations.

Linebacker

The third linebacker position became unsettled when Dee Winters was traded to the Cowboys in the offseason.

Entering training camp, the main contenders were Luke Gifford, who played the position last year and was a Pro Bowler for special teams; Nick Martin, drafted in 2025 but injured much of last year; Garret Wallow, who played well in relief last year; and rookie 5th-round pick Jaden Dugger, who is the most talented of the four.

Gifford has been out for weeks. Martin went down with an injury two games ago. Wallow was out with an injury Thursday night. Dugger was one of the frontrunners to begin with, and he was going to make the team, but probably only one of the others will have a spot. Wallow and Martin have shown promise. Gifford is great on special teams. Will this come down to who will return soonest? If there is a tie in that regard, which one is most likely to clear waivers? (There is no doubt that Shanahan and Lynch want both Martin and Wallow on at least the practice squad.)

So we have four candidates and three injuries.

If a larger pool of IR players were allowed, the situation would be easier, though still difficult.

But the 49ers have to decide only a few days before leaving for Australia who is even able to practice (some of these players are currently in the concussion protocol), let alone play in a game.

And while other GMs and head coaches have the luxury of scanning the waiver wire and having any pickups practice for over a week before the season begins, the Niners will already be acclimating to the time change over 7,000 miles away. Which player can they sign and bring that distance and get up to speed before game day?

I do not envy the kind of situation Lynch and Shanahan are in. No other coach or GM in the league does, either.

title: CHIEFS DRAFT CAPITAL, OR: HOW TO TURN PREMIUM PICKS INTO PREMIUM MEDICAL BILLS
description:
): Felix Anudike-Uzomah (2023 Round 1): Placed on season-ending IR on August 18, 2025, after suffering a catastrophic, severe hamstring tear during preseason camp.
Rashee Rice (2023 Round 2): Placed on season-ending IR following a torn LCL and hamstring tendon damage in Week 4 of the 2024 season.
Wanya Morris (2023 Round 3): Suffered a season-ending knee injury against the Houston Texans in Week 14 of the 2025 season.
Josh Simmons (2025 Round 1): Landed on IR after sustaining a dislocated and fractured wrist in Week 13 against Dallas, requiring major reconstructive surgery.
Because across the NFL, the baseline rate of early-round draft picks (Rounds 1–3) suffering a true season-ending injury during their rookie contract window hovers between 15% and 20%.
text:
I’m not a doctor, but I play one on TV. Maybe you’ve even seen my show - I’m the impossibly handsome resident who’s had a ‘fling’ with every nurse on the ward (except for the token “heavy-set” one with the heart of gold, because I’m way too superficial to be attracted to someone’s personality - SPOILER ALERT!- that won’t happen until season 6). But enough about me (for now, anyway)...

What I’m trying to tell you is that I lack the credentials and training to offer anything meaningful to a discussion about medicine and health (or lack thereof). But, as you by now have probably surmised - I’m going to talk about it anyway.

I’ve been following the news about Josh Simmons’ back problems, and the conspiracy theories that are gaining steam about how he might be exaggerating the injury to avoid playing. I’ve also read the hypothesis (which, rightfully or wrongfully, got over with the Arrowhead Pride fundamentalists about as well as a pregnant pole-vaulter) that Simmons' back problems might be attributable to his off-season weight loss and muscle building program. I’m not going to offer an opinion about that because, as I noted earlier, I’m only a TV doctor. I’ll say this, though - it was actually kind of refreshing to see a Chiefs offensive tackle report to camp not looking like he trained in the off-season at Golden Corral.

Anyway, the discussion about Simmons’ back injury (which followed his season-ending wrist injury, which followed his season-ending torn patellar tendon injury, which followed his season-ending hyperextended earlobe injury) caused me to realize something:

Between the 2023 and 2025 NFL Drafts, the Chiefs made nine selections across the first three rounds - and of those nine premium picks, six have landed on season-ending injured reserve.

I couldn’t even make that up. Here’s what it looks like on paper - presuming you printed this off and filed it in a binder, like many of my readers do. Otherwise you might just be reading it on your phone (Oh, I see how it is - you’re a casual reader. Well… excusez-moi.):

Felix Anudike-Uzomah (2023 Round 1): Placed on season-ending IR on August 18, 2025, after suffering a catastrophic, severe hamstring tear during preseason camp.

Rashee Rice (2023 Round 2): Placed on season-ending IR following a torn LCL and hamstring tendon damage in Week 4 of the 2024 season.

Wanya Morris (2023 Round 3): Suffered a season-ending knee injury against the Houston Texans in Week 14 of the 2025 season.

Kingsley Suamataia (2024 Round 2): Had his campaign cut short by a season-ending ankle injury.

Josh Simmons (2025 Round 1): Landed on IR after sustaining a dislocated and fractured wrist in Week 13 against Dallas, requiring major reconstructive surgery.

Omarr Norman-Lott (2025 Round 2): Tore his right ACL in Week 7 against the Las Vegas Raiders and was placed on season-ending IR on October 21, 2025.

Toss in Ashton Gillotte (2025 Round 3), who’s currently on the shelf with a ruptured plantar fascia (granted, not a season ending injury) in camp, and Xavier Worthy (2024 Round 1), who played the entire 2025 season with one shoulder, and you have yourself a fascinating anomaly.

I know what you must be thinking: What’s an anomaly, Mojo? You know I don’t like it when you use those fancy words!

Sorry…. I forgot about that. An anomaly, simply put, is something that isn’t supposed to happen. Sixty-six percent of the Chiefs’ nine selections across the first three rounds in 2023, 2024, and 2025 have landed on season-ending injured reserve. That - isn’t supposed to happen.

Why do I say that?

Because across the NFL, the baseline rate of early-round draft picks (Rounds 1–3) suffering a true season-ending injury during their rookie contract window hovers between 15% and 20%.

Now, the nitpicker in you (not to be confused with the ‘nosepicker’ in you) will inevitably point to the calendar and claim that some of these designations were administrative conveniences—that guys like Wanya Morris or Josh Simmons only landed on IR because their injuries happened in December when only a handful of regular-season games remained. Go ahead - say it. You know you want to.... Because that’s just what you do, isn't it! You refuse to accept anything I say at face value!! It’s okay. I don’t take personally…. NOSEPICKER!!!

Anyway, that argument completely ignores the surgical reality of the injuries.

When Simmons fractured and dislocated his wrist against Dallas in Week 13, he underwent a complex surgical repair requiring multi-month recovery and rehab. When Morris got rolled up on against the Texans, his knee suffered severe structural trauma requiring full repair. These weren’t your typical, garden-variety soft-tissue tweaks - even if these injuries had occurred in Week 2 or Week 6, they would have ended a season.

And no, I didn’t perform the surgeries. I’m just a TV doctor.

So you might ask: What’s the root cause of all this, Mojo? And I’ll say the same thing to you that I always said to my 9th grade chemistry teacher when she called on me to answer a question in class - “I dunno.... -under my breath- you hateful shrew.”

And I don’t know.

Not for certain.

And I also realize that must come as a complete shock to you because you’ve always operated on the assumption that I know everything about everything.

“Mojo, I feel so disillusioned. I can’t believe in anything anymore!!!!”

What I can infer is that picking at the tail end of the round for the better part of the last decade has led Brett Veach and Andy Reid to take some calculated gambles on players with a premier ceiling over clean medical histories. And that’s understandable - to an extent. We've all bought Ferraris with salvage titles at some point in our lives. And sometimes that strategy can work out magnificently cough cough Trey Smith cough cough. But when six out of nine top selections across three consecutive drafts either lose a full year to major surgery or play through a torn joint capsule, you aren't just dealing with normal football attrition.

You're watching an episode of M*A*S*H.

And even M*A*S*H. eventually got cancelled, so maybe it’s time to switch things up a little.
