title: Projecting the Falcons final 53-man roster and practice squad - The Falcoholic
description:
The third and final preseason game is over, and it’s time for our final roster predictions.
UDFA Jack Strand has consistently impressed through training camp and the preseason, and I simply can’t imagine risking him on the practice squad.
The biggest riser is Branch, who dominated throughout training camp and preseason and is likely to take over the WR3 role.
Samson Ebukam and Cameron Thomas had a nice training camp, and both seem to be working primarily with the starters.
Da’Shawn Hand suffered an injury early in training camp, but was drawing rave reviews from the coaching staff before then.
text:
The third and final preseason game is over, and it’s time for our final roster predictions. Cutdowns are a lot earlier this year—Sunday instead of Tuesday—which means there’s little time for consideration. Accordingly, I’ll be trying to get this to you all as early as possible on Saturday. The Dolphins game didn’t provide many new insights, but how the snaps were divvied out might provide some clues as to where certain players stand.

Let’s dive right in to my final thoughts on Atlanta’s 2026 53-man roster. The roster projection is also available in both video and audio format, which you can find embedded below. If you enjoyed the written version, consider giving us a click on these platforms as well.

Listen to the audio version of this article using the player below, or find it on your favorite podcast platforms.

Italics denote a change from the previous roster projection.

OFFENSE - 25

Quarterback - 4

Michael Penix Jr.

Tua Tagovailoa

Cooper Rush

Jack Strand

The Tua vs Penix camp battle has been anticlimactic, to say the least. Tua started out camp fine, but has struggled since the start of the preseason. The fact that he hasn’t taken control of the starting job at this point is fairly telling. Meanwhile, Penix just returned to full 11-on-11 work on Monday, and is having a bit of an adjustment period. There’s just enough time for Penix to win the starting job before Week 1, and I think he will ultimately do so. Put simply, the Falcons have a lot more incentive to put Penix on the field, assuming he’s healthy and ready to go.

The most interesting battle of the offseason might actually be at the bottom of the depth chart at quarterback. UDFA Jack Strand has consistently impressed through training camp and the preseason, and I simply can’t imagine risking him on the practice squad. Cooper Rush remains a steady veteran option and is not subject to waivers, but at least initially, I think both begin on the roster. Shuffling will be likely in the coming days.

Running Back - 3

Bijan Robinson

Brian Robinson

Tyler Goodson

I’m really excited to see what Bijan Robinson can do in this offense. The Falcons offensive line is still working on incorporating more power concepts into the rushing attack, but once they’ve got it down, I think Robinson might be in line for his best season yet. He’ll also be heavily involved as a pass catching option, and I expect to see a lot of stuff schemed up for Robinson.

Brian Robinson is a steady veteran who more or less replicates Tyler Allgeier’s role, just at a fraction of the price. I wouldn’t expect Robinson to match Allgeier’s play, but he’ll be fine. The pleasant surprise of the offseason has been the emergence of Tyler Goodson, who looks like a legitimate threat as a runner, pass catcher, and returner. Impressive UDFA Cash Jones could also be in consideration here if Atlanta opts for more RBs.

Tight End - 4

Kyle Pitts

Charlie Woerner

Austin Hooper

Nick Muse

The Falcons are going to run their fair share of 12 personnel packages this season, which is why I favor the team keeping 4 TEs over 4 RBs or 6 WRs. Kyle Pitts looks to be in line for a featured role, and I expect his target share to be a lot more consistent in Tommy Rees’ offense. Charlie Woerner will be the primary blocking tight end, and he offers a unique skillset there. Austin Hooper will be the secondary receiving tight end, and may end up playing a similar number of snaps to Woerner.

A big surprise has been the play of recently-signed Nick Muse and UDFA Jack Velling. Both were excellent as blockers and receivers against the Colts, and are making a serious push for the roster over Joshua Simon. At this point, I give the slight lead to Muse, but it’s close.

Wide Receiver - 5

Drake London

Jahan Dotson

Zachariah Branch

Olamide Zaccheaus

Chris Blair

One of the biggest developments of the summer is Atlanta’s high usage of 11 personnel (3 WR sets), and the quality of their receiving corps in general. 2025’s unit was among the NFL’s worst due to injury, mismanagement, and a lack of coaching. Things turned around quickly thanks to two veteran additions and the addition of electric rookie Zachariah Branch, and as a result, we could see a lot more receivers on the field than originally anticipated.

Drake London will continue to dominate targets and remains the top pass catcher on the roster. His size and physicality stand out in a room filled with smaller, speedier options. Jahan Dotson acquitted himself well in training camp and seems to have the WR2 job locked up thanks to his experience, route running prowess, and versatility to play outside or in the slot. The biggest riser is Branch, who dominated throughout training camp and preseason and is likely to take over the WR3 role. Veteran Olamide Zaccheaus is a quality rotational option who provides depth in the slot and at returner. Chris Blair finally seems to have a staff who actually recognizes his talent, and is likely to be a fixture on special teams and as Drake London’s primary backup.

Offensive Line - 9

LT Jake Matthews

LG Matthew Bergeron

C Ryan Neuzil

RG Chris Lindstrom

RT Jawaan Taylor

T Michael Jerrell

T/G Ethan Onianwa

C/G Corey Levin

T Wanya Morris

IR: Kyle Hinton

The Falcons have four solid starters on the offensive line all returning from 2025, and one big question mark in right tackle Jawaan Taylor. We’ve hardly seen Taylor this summer, but he appears fully healthy now and should be a meaningful upgrade over the depth tackles and 2025 starter Elijah Wilkinson. Taylor’s play will determine both the ceiling and floor of this line, and it’ll be up to Bill Callahan to see if he can squeeze more run blocking prowess out of the veteran.

Most of the intrigue in this group is with the depth players, as there’s been a pretty fierce battle for swing tackle. Michael Jerrell has more or less manned the swing tackle spot since the start of training camp, and rebounded with a strong performance against the Colts after a rough outing against the Broncos. He’s not an overly inspiring option, but at least he’s shown some improvement. The shocker might by trade acquisition Wanya Morris falling behind rookie Ethan Onianwa. Onianwa got the bulk of the right tackle reps in both preseason games, with Morris being relegated to the depth unit. The rookie was legitimately impressive against the Colts and is learning quickly—I think he gets the roster nod, in part due to his draft status.

There’s a bit of intrigue with the depth guards, as both Kyle Hinton and UDFA Kam Dewberry played pretty well thus far. Hinton is apparently in a large knee brace and didn’t participate in the third preseason game: he might be headed to IR, short-term or otherwise. Dewberry is someone to watch as a developmental practice squad player. Veteran Corey Levin looks like the far superior center option (who also offers guard flexibility), with UDFA James Brockermeyer struggling through the preseason.

DEFENSE - 25

Edge Defender - 5

Za’Darius Smith

Samson Ebukam

Cameron Thomas

Azeez Ojulari

Bralen Trice

SUSPENDED: James Pearce Jr.

We officially got word on an eight-game suspension for James Pearce Jr., and the Falcons will struggle to generate pressure off the edge in his absence. As a result of the suspension and Jalon Walker’s season-ending injury, Atlanta brought in veteran Za’Darius Smith to bolster the room. I’m not sure what to expect from Smith entering his age 34 season, but by all accounts he’s impressed the coaching staff early and has brought a lot of veteran swagger to the room. At worst, he’s a good run defender who can also bring some juice on passing downs.

I still like Atlanta’s rotational rushers, though they’re going to be relied upon a lot more than expected with the team’s top two edge players out. Samson Ebukam and Cameron Thomas had a nice training camp, and both seem to be working primarily with the starters. Ebukam offers a bit more as a pass rusher, Thomas a bit more as a run defender. Azeez Ojulari was mostly quiet in camp, but has been a solid pass rusher during the preseason. We’ll see if Bralen Trice can hold onto the lead he established early in camp, but his lack of preseason snaps may see the team pivot to intriguing UFL signing Keshawn Banks.

Interior Defensive Line - 5

Brandon Dorlus

Zach Harrison

LaCale London

Da’Shawn Hand

Maason Smith

The Falcons interior defensive line continues to be one of the most underrated units in football. Brandon Dorlus was one of the NFL’s best interior pass rushers before injury in 2025, and has continued to impress this summer. Zach Harrison finally returned to the field at the start of the preseason, and has been getting a lot of reps to help him get back up to speed. He’s split time on the interior and on the edge, and has been looking great against opposing 2s. Hopefully he’s 100% by the time Week 1 arrives. LaCale London missed the first two preseason games but is coming off a very effective season as a rotational player and figures to continue in that role.

Da’Shawn Hand suffered an injury early in training camp, but was drawing rave reviews from the coaching staff before then. I expect he’ll be a key player for Atlanta on early downs, and should return in time for Week 1. The biggest disappointment is probably trade acquisition Maason Smith, who has looked disruptive as a pass rusher but hasn’t made his mark as a run defender. The upside is obvious and there’s still plenty of room for development.

Linebacker - 5

Divine Deablo

Kendal Daniels

Christian Harris

Harold Perkins Jr.

Josh Woods

Divine Deablo returned from a minor injury sustained in the second week of training camp and should continue to be one of the best and most important players on defense. Rookie Kendal Daniels shot up the depth chart over the course of camp and the preseason, and now looks to be in line to start next to Deablo in Week 1. Veteran Christian Harris is a terrific third linebacker with a lot of coverage talent—it’s more of a testament to Daniels’ play than Harris faltering this summer. Harold Perkins Jr., the other rookie linebacker, also figures to have a rotational role as a pass rush specialist while he continues to find his footing as a off-ball player. Veteran Josh Woods is a special teams standout and passable depth player on defense, and I think he’s outplayed JD Bertrand and Channing Tindall for this final spot.

Cornerback - 6

A.J. Terrell

Mike Hughes

Avieon Terrell

C.J. Henderson

Darnay Holmes

Mike Ford Jr.

PUP: Billy Bowman Jr.

A.J. Terrell gives the Falcons a legitimate lockdown corner to play against the top receiving talent in the league, while Mike Hughes seems to have taken a step forward as a CB2 based on a very strong training camp performance. Avieon Terrell steadily rose up the depth chart in camp, splitting time between outside and slot duties, but missed the first two preseason games with a minor injury. It seems like Avieon is being prepared to play the slot, and if he’s not starting there in Week 1, he will be within a few weeks.

Atlanta seems to have some quality depth behind the starting trio. C.J. Henderson, the former first-rounder, has impressed through camp and preseason on the outside. Veteran Darnay Holmes took over the slot starter job at the start of the preseason, in part due to Terrell’s absence, and hasn’t looked back. He’s been pretty solid and gives the team a bit of insurance in case Avieon isn’t quite up to speed due to injury recovery. The sixth cornerback job is wide open, and that makes me lean towards special teams ace Mike Ford Jr. He’s a terrific special teamer, although you don’t want to see him on defense. This could also be Clark Phillips III (if the team doesn’t mind paying him the salary) or intriguing UDFA Malcolm DeWalt IV (if the team is looking for developmental upside). Unfortunately, Cobee Bryant seems to have played himself out of roster contention. He remains too grabby, and that’s just something you can’t get away with in the NFL.

Safety - 4

Jessie Bates III

Xavier Watts

Sydney Brown

DeMarcco Hellams

While we haven’t seen much of Jessie Bates III in training camp or the preseason, I’d expect him to be full go for Week 1. Alongside second-year dynamo Xavier Watts, the Falcons should once again have one of the best safety duos in the league. That gives Atlanta a lot of flexibility to play more aggressively up front, which is welcome given the injuries/suspensions in the edge room.

Trade acquisition Sydney Brown has established himself as the third safety, and seems to have a role carved out as a “big nickel” in certain packages. While I thought he might lose his grip on the roster this summer, DeMarcco Hellams instead turned in a great camp and even better preseason. He looks more disciplined in coverage and is playing smarter while retaining his physical brand of play.

SPECIAL TEAMS - 3

K Nick Folk

P Jake Bailey

LS Liam McCullough

RETURNERS

KR Zachariah Branch/Tyler Goodson

PR Zachariah Branch

Nick Folk has been tremendous as both a field goal kicker and a kickoff specialist through the preseason. Hopefully he can continue at this level for the next few years. New punter Jake Bailey also delivered some fantastic plays and looks like an upgrade over the (still) perennially underrated Bradley Pinion. I still expect Zachariah Branch to be Atlanta’s top return specialist on punts and kickoffs thanks to his dynamic ability, but the most pleasant surprise in that competition has been Tyler Goodson. Goodson’s talents seem to translate well to returns, and I think he might end up the secondary kickoff returner for the Falcons to start the season.

PRACTICE SQUAD - 16

RB Cash Jones

WR Vinny Anthony II

WR Dylan Drummond

TE Jack Velling

TE Josh Simon

T Brandon Walton

G Kam Dewberry

C James Brockermeyer

EDGE Keshawn Banks

DT Chris Williams

DT Carlos Allen Jr.

LB JD Bertrand

CB Clark Phillips III

CB A.J. Woods

CB Malcolm DeWalt IV

S Jammie Robinson

What are your thoughts on this potential roster for the Falcons? Any changes you’d make?

title: Eagles final 53-man roster projection: Who wins backup QB job? Who lands the final spots?
description:
The Philadelphia Eagles now must choose their 53-man roster and 16-man practice squad by the NFL’s 6 p.m.
Unless GM Howie Roseman makes a trade here, it behooves the Eagles to keep Dalton around on the practice squad.
That covers all the possibilities, which suggests a lack of clarity after five weeks of training camp.
Cooper has been a training camp standout who went from the roster bubble to sitting in the final preseason game.
Lampkin and Kendall’s strong showing in training camp showed the Eagles can feel confident in their interior backup options.
text:
PHILADELPHIA — Training camp is over. The preseason film is filed. The Philadelphia Eagles now must choose their 53-man roster and 16-man practice squad by the NFL’s 6 p.m. ET Sunday deadline.

The Athletic’s Zach Berman and Brooks Kubena make their final roster predictions.

Quarterbacks

Kubena (3): Jalen Hurts, Tanner McKee, Cole Payton

This is as precarious as the quarterback depth has been in coach Nick Sirianni’s tenure. There was no clear winner in the backup battle between Tanner McKee and Andy Dalton. Both quarterbacks fared better against the opponent’s third-team defenses in the last two exhibitions. McKee had his chance to seize the QB2 spot by starting against the Cincinnati Bengals on Friday night, and he went 12 of 22 passing for 55 yards and an interception. Unless GM Howie Roseman makes a trade here, it behooves the Eagles to keep Dalton around on the practice squad. McKee, a 2023 sixth-round pick, would be subject to waivers if cut.

Worth noting: Cole Payton was in the backfield with the punt coverage team. It appears the Eagles, who liked Payton’s athleticism coming out of North Dakota State, are finding additional value in the fifth-round rookie if they keep him on the 53-man roster.

Berman (3): Jalen Hurts, Tanner McKee, Cole Payton

This could go in any direction. Neither McKee nor Dalton did enough to win the No. 2 job. Does McKee keep it based on what he’s demonstrated in Philadelphia in the past? Does Dalton stay because of experience — or does that enhance his trade value to a backup-needy team? Then again, the Eagles might be a backup-needy team. Would Roseman seek a trade of his own — Anthony Richardson or J.J. McCarthy are former first-rounders who could benefit from a change of scenery. Roseman could also keep all four quarterbacks to maintain his bluff. That covers all the possibilities, which suggests a lack of clarity after five weeks of training camp. Payton has more versatility than a typical depth quarterback, which could make him an intriguing option to develop a Taysom Hill-like role.

Running backs

Kubena (3): Saquon Barkley, Tank Bigsby, Will Shipley

This trio was never truly challenged in training camp. Carson Steele had an impressive game against the Patriots and recorded another touchdown catch against the Bengals. Dameon Pierce, debuting after missing time with a hamstring injury, showcased his power running style by gaining 44 yards on four carries. There doesn’t seem to be room for either player on this initial roster. But they could make for interesting additions to the practice squad — and useful foils for the defense as members of the scout team unit.

Berman (3): Saquon Barkley, Tank Bigsby, Will Shipley

These three are all locks, as evidenced by Nick Sirianni keeping the trio sidelined for the final game. Both Carson Steele and Dameon Pierce showed ability during the preseason, but I don’t see the Eagles keeping more than three.

Wide receivers

Kubena (5): DeVonta Smith, Dontayvion Wicks, Hollywood Brown, Makai Lemon, Darius Cooper

Darius Cooper did not suit up Friday night — an indication that he has all but sealed a spot on the 53-man roster for a second straight year. Cooper has graduated from the feel-good training camp story. It will be interesting to see how much he progresses as a pass-catcher in Year 2. Elijah Moore did suit up Friday and is a sensible practice-squad option because none of his $1.3 million contract is guaranteed. The Eagles can pick up a roster spot if they keep Moore in town.

Berman (5): DeVonta Smith, Dontayvion Wicks, Makai Lemon, Darius Cooper, Hollywood Brown

These five should all be on the team, with Brown’s $5 million guaranteed contract and his quality experience helping his case. Cooper has been a training camp standout who went from the roster bubble to sitting in the final preseason game. The question is whether they keep another receiver such as Moore. I think he’s more likely as a practice squad elevation.

Tight ends

Kubena (3): Dallas Goedert, Johnny Mundt, Eli Stowers

There is little question about the efficacy of Goedert and Mundt when they are both on the field. But it does not yet look like the Eagles can rely on Stowers to provide them with the depth they need at this position. The second-round rookie still needs to progress as a blocker. It also does not help that he missed the last three training camp practices, plus Friday night’s preseason finale, with a hamstring injury. Is the best backup on the roster? Practice squad mainstays Cam Latu and E.J. Jenkins both have dropped passes in training camp. Stone Smartt totaled seven catches for 47 yards in the final two exhibitions.

Berman (4): Dallas Goedert, Johnny Mundt, Eli Stowers, Cameron Latu

Stowers has had a quiet camp, and an injury last week kept him out of the preseason finale. Depending on the severity of Stowers’ injury, pay attention to his roster status to begin the season. Latu has not necessarily excelled this summer and is the last player on this 53-man roster, but his special teams value and versatility as a fullback put him on the list. It wouldn’t surprise me if Roseman seeks an upgrade for the tight end depth chart — especially with the Eagles expected to play heavy packages. Do the Eagles call Zach Ertz and allow him to finish his career in Philadelphia?

Offensive line

Kubena (10): Lane Johnson, Jordan Mailata, Markel Bell, Fred Johnson, Cam Jurgens, Landon Dickerson, Tyler Steen, Drew Kendall, Willie Lampkin, Micah Morris

The rookie Bell missed the final three training camp practices and the preseason finale with a thumb/leg injury. This underscores why it makes sense for the Eagles to keep Fred Johnson on the roster as another capable option. Lampkin and Kendall’s strong showing in training camp showed the Eagles can feel confident in their interior backup options. Neither player suited up Friday, which should be taken as a vote of confidence. Will the Eagles need to call upon them this year?

Berman (10): Jordan Mailata, Landon Dickerson, Cam Jurgens, Tyler Steen, Lane Johnson, Fred Johnson, Markel Bell, Drew Kendall, Willie Lampkin, Micah Morris

Fred Johnson is a tough one to figure in this group — especially if Bell is the Eagles’ swing tackle. Fred Johnson could be a trade candidate or even a practice squad player considering he’s a vested veteran. Still, I have him on this 53-man roster to give the Eagles an experienced offensive tackle. Otherwise, the reserves are inexperienced. The Eagles’ interior offensive linemen have demonstrated impressive development this summer; Kendall, Lampkin, and Morris all made strides. I’m watching to see if the Eagles keep Cameron Williams and Myles Hinton for developmental purposes, although neither has shown enough.

Defensive line

Kubena (6): Jalen Carter, Jordan Davis, Moro Ojomo, Byron Young, Ty Robinson, Zion Wilson

I am adding Wilson for the first time. The undrafted rookie from East Carolina finished training camp with a series of impressive practices and recorded a tackle for loss and a quarterback hit in the preseason finale. I think he offers the Eagles more immediate value than Uar Bernard, who defensive coordinator Vic Fangio has said is “light years away” from contributing. Yes, it would be a risk to subject Bernard to the waiver wire. But acquiring him would be a considerable investment for any team. The Eagles could then keep him on their practice squad without counting him against the numbers as a member of the International Pathway Program.

Berman (6): Jalen Carter, Jordan Davis, Moro Ojomo, Byron Young, Ty Robinson, Uar Bernard

Carter, Davis and Ojomo form a trio of DTs at or near the top of the league, while Young is a quality reserve. Bernard was drafted as a long-term project, and I don’t expect the Eagles to expose him to waivers and risk another team absorbing the project. One player to watch out here: Wilson, who has shown positive flashes this summer and is similarly a project as a defensive tackle after converting from offensive line in college.

Edge rushers

Kubena (6): Jonathan Greenard, Jalyx Hunt, Nolan Smith, Arnold Ebiketie, A.J. Epenesa, Joshua Weru

The biggest question here is how much time Greenard misses in the regular season with his pectoral injury. Hunt and Nolan Smith have plenty of starting experience to temporarily hold the line. But there wasn’t any sign in the preseason that Ebiketie and Epenesa bring any volatility as depth players.

Weru, another IPP member, offers the Eagles more immediate value than Bernard. Weru played more than a third of the defense’s total snaps in all three exhibitions, and recorded a sack against New England.

Berman (6): Jonathan Greenard, Jalyx Hunt, Nolan Smith, Arnold Ebiketie, A.J. Epenesa, Joshua Weru

The top five are set — I believe Epenesa will make the roster even if he could be a potential practice squad elevation — and the Eagles should gamble on Weru’s upside and apply similar logic as they would with Bernard. His tools are worth developing, and there’s nobody they need to pound the table to keep ahead of him. Even if he’s far away, the Eagles have the roster flexibility to stash him on the 53. I’m also watching Greenard’s status. My guess is they don’t put him on PUP to begin the season.

Linebackers

Kubena (5): Zack Baun, Jihaad Campbell, Jeremiah Trotter Jr., Smael Mondon Jr., Deontae Lawson

This comes down to whether the Eagles want to keep Chance Campbell or Deontae Lawson. I’ve chosen Chance Campbell throughout my training camp predictions until now. Lawson, an undrafted rookie from Clemson, showed his knack for finding the football by forcing a fumble against the Bengals. Forcing turnovers secures attention. Lawson has progressed in the defensive system throughout training camp, and the upside he’s showcased might be enough for him to be claimed on waivers.

Berman (5): Zack Baun, Jihaad Campbell, Jeremiah Trotter Jr., Smael Mondon Jr., Chance Campbell

This is a deep group of inside linebackers, and I went back and forth between Chance Campbell and Lawson. For a fifth linebacker, the Eagles might prefer the upside of Lawson. Chance Campbell can help on special teams and could offer quality depth if they’re afraid another team would claim him. He was available for the rest of the league to sign last year, and it didn’t happen. This could be one of the tougher debates in the room. Is Mondon a trade candidate?

Cornerbacks

Kubena (6): Quinyon Mitchell, Cooper DeJean, Riq Woolen, Mac McWilliams, Jonathan Jones, Kelee Ringo

Training camp has been rough for the depth members of this position group. If an injury happens to any of the starters, the Eagles could be in considerable trouble. Roseman churned the trade market last season to acquire depth at outside cornerback, and I would not be surprised if he looked for outside help again. It would have helped to see Jones more in action. He missed the majority of camp with a shoulder injury.

Berman (6): Quinyon Mitchell, Cooper DeJean, Riq Woolen, Jonathan Jones, Mac McWilliams, Kelee Ringo

The top three are entrenched in their roles and give the Eagles the best trio in the NFL. The depth behind them has been lacking this summer. Jones’ injury kept him off the field for a chunk of camp, but I think the Eagles need his experience in case of an injury. Ringo’s floor is at least a quality special teams player. I would have liked to see more of Jakorian Bennett this summer, but he’s been sidelined for most of camp.

Safety

Kubena (3): Drew Mukuba, Marcus Epps, Michael Carter II

I’m sticking with three players here. Again, Cooper DeJean is essentially the fourth safety and will play there in base packages. It is unfortunate for the Eagles that Andre’ Sam left Friday’s game on a cart. I saw him scooting past the locker room in the hallway after the game, and his left leg and foot were in a brace.

Sirianni did not offer any updates on Sam’s injury, but Sam may not be immediately available as a practice squad call-up option. Carter played a significant number of snaps on Friday. He started at safety, then moved to nickel. I spoke to him at his locker. Both positions are new to him — although he played nickel with the New York Jets before arriving in Philadelphia via trade — and the plan was to get him more in-game experience.

Berman (3): Drew Mukuba, Marcus Epps, Michael Carter II

Roseman could seek an upgrade because this group seems light. They can go with three because Cooper DeJean plays safety in the base. Still, Carter is new to the position, and if the only depth option is a first-year safety, that could be concerning in the event of an injury. Maximus Pulley and Kapena Gushiken are two undrafted rookies who had their moments.

Specialists

Kubena (3): Jake Elliott, Braden Mann, Rocco Underwood

Welcome back, Rocco. I have made room for thee.

And welcome back, Jake the Make. At least a promising preview of him. He nailed a 56-yarder against the Bengals. He has been 5-for-15 from 50-plus in each of the last two seasons.

Berman (2): Jake Elliott, Braden Mann

In this scenario, the Eagles waive long snapper Rocco Underwood and evaluate the long snapping situation after cut-down day. The Eagles did the same last year. Usually, you’re trying to squeeze players onto the roster. This year, the bottom-of-the-roster depth seems lighter than in previous seasons.

text:
EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — Chip Trayanum was taken to a hospital with a neck injury after earlier running for a touchdown in the New York Jets’ 23-6 preseason loss to the Giants on Friday night.

The Jets announced that Trayanum, an undrafted rookie running back from Toledo, was awake, alert and had movement in his extremities.

“I think he’ll be just fine,” coach Aaron Glenn said after the game. “He’ll be just fine.”

Trayanum saw extended snaps and finished with 38 yards on 12 carries as Glenn and the Giants’ John Harbaugh rested almost all of their projected starters. With 10 seconds remaining before halftime and with the ball deep in their own territory, the Jets opted to hand it off to Trayanum — who was immediately walloped by Trace Ford.

Jets players and coaches remained on the field — many on their knees and praying — as Trayanum was examined in a scary and eerily quiet scene at MetLife Stadium. He was put in a neck brace, strapped to a backboard and loaded onto a cart and driven off the field.

The 24-year-old native of Akron, Ohio, played a major role on offense early with the Jets (1-2).

After Marcelino McCrary-Ball intercepted Jameis Winston — who started in place of Jaxson Dart — on a pass intended for Odell Beckham Jr. that was deflected by Qwan’tez Stiggers, the Jets’ offense hit the ground running.

Literally.

The Jets ran on 10 straight plays, including nine by Trayanum, who capped the drive with 1-yard touchdown run. Rookie quarterback Cade Klubnik, starting in place of Geno Smith, had the other rush on a 6-yard scramble.

Jason Sanders, who won the Jets’ kicker competition this week by beating out Cade York, was wide left on the extra point. He also was short on a 54-yard field-goal attempt.

With the Giants (2-1) driving deep in Jets territory on their next possession, McCrary-Ball punched the ball out of Braxton Berrios’ hands and Stiggers recovered in the end zone for a touchback.

The Jets couldn’t take advantage and went three-and-out. A 16-yard run by Tyrone Tracy and a 23-yard catch by Beckham got the Giants to the 6, and Tracy ran it in to put the Giants up 7-6 with 28 seconds left in the opening quarter.

Klubnik has a so-so showing in his bid to be the Jets’ No. 2 QB

Klubnik, a fourth-round pick, was intercepted early in the second quarter by Zaire Barnes, a sixth-rounder of the Jets in 2023 who signed with the Giants last year. It was Klubnik’s first turnover of the preseason.

He played the entire first half and was 6 of 13 for 59 yards and the INT. He was replaced by Bailey Zappe to start the third quarter.

“Overall, not my best ball,” Klubnik said.

Glenn said Klubnik was “up and down” and declined to declare him the No. 2 quarterback behind Smith.

Beckham almost makes a sparkling play like the OBJ of old

Beckham, possibly looking to secure a roster spot, caught three passes for 53 yards on six targets in the first half. But he nearly had an amazing catch.

Early in the second quarter, Beckham got behind the coverage and Winston threw a deep pass that appeared on its way to being a 73-yard touchdown. But the ball was slightly overthrown and Beckham dived, but it went off his fingertips when he hit the ground.

“I don’t want to say exactly that he’s making it right now or not, what the considerations are, and things can happen,” Harbaugh said. “But I think I would answer the question, yes, I think he has done enough to make an NFL roster, for sure. He’s played well.”

The 33-year-old Beckham, a first-round pick of the Giants in 2014 who played five seasons with the franchise, re-signed with his original team in June. His chances of making the roster improved when Calvin Austin tore the ACL in his right knee earlier this week.

“Super grateful for the opportunity,” Beckham said. “At this point, it’s in God’s hands. I know that I have a good feeling about myself. I feel like there’s ball to be played, plays to be made.”

Haener leads late TD drive for Giants

Jake Haener, fourth on the Giants’ depth chart behind Dart, Winston and Brandon Allen, had a 37-yard touchdown pass to Xavier Gipson in the fourth quarter.

Haener, who spent his first three NFL seasons with New Orleans, signed with the Giants last week.

Zvada wins Giants’ kicking competition

Harbaugh announced that rookie Dominic Zvada won the Giants’ kicker job, beating out Ben Sauls.

Zvada kicked field goals of 23, 53 and 46 yards against the Jets and made both of his extra points.

Injuries

Giants: Tracy left in the second quarter to be evaluated for a concussion, but was cleared to return.

Jets: Glenn said CB Tre Brown was taken to a hospital because of a finger injury. … Edge rusher Joseph Ossai left in the first quarter with a foot injury. … Rookie G Anez Cooper, a sixth-round pick, was ruled out after injuring his right shoulder in the second quarter. … WR Cam Camper was evaluated for a concussion in the second half and cleared. … RB Dominic Richardson injured an elbow in the fourth quarter.

Up next

Giants: Host Dallas in a Sunday night matchup on Sept. 13.

Jets: Take on former coach Robert Saleh and the Titans in Tennessee on Sept. 13.

text:
During what was a heated practice between the Tennessee Titans and Chicago Bears on Thursday, Wan’Dale Robinson was forced to leave early.

Robinson took what Titans head coach Robert Saleh deemed a “cheap” hit from Bears safety Xavier Woods, which led to the wideout undergoing concussion tests.

Thankfully, there’s good news to report on the veteran wide receiver after initial testing.

According to NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport, Robinson was checked for a concussion and it is believed he has avoided one.

“Titans WR Wan’Dale Robinson, who was checked for a concussion yesterday after joint practice, is not believed to have suffered one, source says,” Rapoport reported.

MORE: Wan’Dale Robinson is the 2026 fantasy football sleeper of the year

“The team will continue to monitor him to make sure concussions symptoms don’t arise. But positive early indications,” he added.

As Rapoport notes, it’s not impossible for concussion symptoms to pop up, but for now, it looks like Robinson is doing OK.

Robinson is coming off a career year in 2025 that saw him post 92 catches for 1,014 yards and four touchdowns with the New York Giants.

When it was all said and done, Robinson ranked as WR14 overall, according to Fantasy Pros.

However, that showing comes with a very important caveat, as Robinson was the top target in a wide receivers room devoid of talent after the season-ending injury to Malik Nabers.

Now with the Titans in 2026, Robinson’s outlook isn’t as positive.

MORE: Josh Downs & 6 more fantasy football wide receiver sleepers for 2026

Not only does he have to catch passes from Cam Ward, who had a disappointing rookie season, he also has a good amount of competition for targets.

Flanking Robinson will be first-round pick Carnell Tate and veteran Calvin Ridley, and tight end Gunnar Helm should have a sizable role, also.

One thing Robinson does have working for him is that he’s reunited with his former head coach and play-caller, Brian Daboll, who is Tennessee’s offensive coordinator.

MORE: Bhayshul Tuten is fantasy football’s next breakout running back in 2026

The familiarity between Daboll and Robinson could give the veteran a leg up in Tennessee’s offensive game plan.

We’re extremely skeptical that Robinson is going to be able to re-create what he did last season given what we know about Ward and Robinson’s competition for targets.

Pencil Robinson in as a low-end flex option until we see him consistently produce in Nashville.

text:
Our New England Patriots roster projection 3.0 was supposed to be our final one of the summer. So much for that.

That roster projection went out after the Patriots' second preseason game against the Eagles. A lot has happened since then. Part of that is updates on injuries from that game, but also the team holding two practices and having an additional preseason game since.

Typically we don't do a roster projection after the preseason finale since the team gets right into roster cuts. With some much changing though, we'll try to squeeze in an update to 3.0 before the moves start getting made.

One note as well - we typically do this projections to reflect the immediate roster after the 6:00 deadline. For this projection, we're looking through waiver claims the days following.

Rookies are in italics

Quarterbacks (3)

-Drake Maye

-Tommy DeVito

-Behren Morton

Changes from 3.0: None

While Morton struggled in the preseason finale, his overall body of work this summer was a positive. Plus, there's value in carrying a third quarterback for the emergency third QB gameday rule.

Running backs (3)

-Rhamondre Stevenson

-TreVeyon Henderson

-Lan Larison

Changes from 3.0: ADD Lan Larison, CUT Hassan Haskins

There are two factors that go into making this change. One is the fact that Henderson missed the week after leaving Monday's practice early with a foot/ankle injury. Larison is more of a do-it-all back that can take some of the responsibilities off Henderson's plate if needed. The Patriots also gave Larison a more limited role on Thursday night, with Mike Vrabel noting after the game a point of emphasis was for the Patriots "to try to get to the regular season with the guys that we had." Haskins remains a practice squad candidate.

Wide receivers (6)

-A.J. Brown

-Romeo Doubs

-DeMario Douglas

-Mack Hollins

-Kyle Williams

-Efton Chism

Changes from 3.0: None

We haven't moved off of this projection all summer, and there's no reason to do so now. It's chalk here, with the Patriots' deepest position group.

Tight ends/fullback (4)

-Hunter Henry

-Eli Raridon

-Tanner Arkin

-Reggie Gilliam (FB)

Changes from 3.0: None

The Patriots are most likely going to carry three tight ends. Arkin has done enough to earn a roster spot, but hasn't played at the level that he's beyond replaceable. Finding an upgrade on waivers with the 31st priority spot might be tough, but not impossible. We have him on for now, but his spot isn't fully secure.

Offensive line (9)

-T Will Campbell

-T Morgan Moses

-G Alijah Vera-Tucker

-G Mike Onwenu

-C Jared Wilson

-T Marcus Bryant

-T/G Caleb Lomu

-T Dametrious Crownover

-G/C Greg Van Roten

IR: Ben Brown

Changes from 3.0: None

The urgency in which the Patriots seem to be preparing Van Roten - including having him play center in practice this week - could be a sign Brown won't be ready to start the season. He'll have to miss at least four weeks by going on IR, but that move opens a roster spot elsewhere. Meanwhile James Hudson has worked his way back onto the bubble, notably playing tackle on Thursday night following Marcus Bryant's injury. Hudson spent most of the summer at guard, and is a strong candidate for a veteran practice squad spot.

Defensive line (5)

-Milton Williams

-Christian Barmore

-Cory Durden

-Joshua Farmer

-Eric Gregory

Changes from 3.0: None

The top four players here all feel like roster locks. Gregory has the edge on the next group of players for the final spot, given what he brings as a run defender. Leonard Taylor and Jeremiah Pharms could be in the mix too and are strong practice squad candidates.

Edge rushers (5)

-Dre'Mont Jones

-Gabe Jacas

-Elijah Ponder

-Quintayvious Hutchins

-TBD edge rusher

PUP: Harold Landry

Changes from 3.0: ADD Quintayvious Hutchins and TBD edge rusher, PUP Harold Landry

With less than two weeks to go until the opener, it feels increasingly unlikely that Landry will be able to return. The Patriots can leave him on PUP, which would rule him out for at least the first four weeks of the season. Still, the team needs bodies at the position, especially as Jacas continues to catch up to the pace of the NFL game. Hutchins gets one spot having had the best camp of the Patriots' remaining in house options, plus his special teams ability. At the same time, this is a spot where the Patriots should be looking at external additions on waivers or elsewhere.

Linebackers (4)

-Robert Spillane

-Christian Elliss

-TBD Linebaker

-K.J. Britt

IR: Khalil Jacobs

Changes from 3.0: ADD TBD linebacker, IR Khalil Jacobs, CUT Chad Muma

Linebacker is another spot where the Patriots should be looking for an external addition. Jacobs could help bolster the depth if healthy, but he didn't practice this week after getting hurt again the Eagles. Meanwhile Muma played late into Thursday night's game against the Browns, which is not an encouraging sign to conclude what's been a rough preseason overall.

Cornerbacks (6)

-Christian Gonzalez

-Carlton Davis

-Marcus Jones

-Charles Woods

-Kindle Vildor

-Karon Prunty

Changes from 3.0: None

Woods, Vildor, and Prunty are all in the mix for the top backup cornerback job, yet none have separated themselves. Woods has the experience in the system, Vildor had a good week against the Eagles (but struggled against the Browns), and Prunty has athletic upside and special teams ability. For now we have the Patriots keeping all three, with the battle continuing into the start of the season until they need another roster spot.

Safeties (5)

-Kevin Byard

-Craig Woodson

-Jaylen Reed

-Dell Pettus

-John Saunders Jr.

NFI: Brenden Schooler

Changes from 3.0: ADD Jaylen Reed, NFI Brenden Schooler

Will the Patriots keep four or five safeties? Reed adds an extra layer of depth that could put Pettus or Saunders on the edge. Reed is more stylistically similar to Pettus, but Saunders did play late into Thursday night's game.

Specialists (3)

-K Andy Borregales

-P Bryce Baringer

-LS Julian Ashby

Changes from 3.0: None

Unless Bryce Baringer's injury is more serious than it seems right now (it's worth noting he stayed in uniform and continued holding against the Eagles) the Patriots may not want to rule him out for four games with an IR placement. If he can't go for the opener, the Patriots should be able to get Matt Haack to the practice squad and elevate him from there.

On the bubble

-EDGE Quintayvious Hutchins

-DT Eric Gregory

-S John Saunders Jr.

The Bears received encouraging injury news recently, with Ozzy Trapilo coming off the active/PUP list and getting in more than a week’s worth of practices. It will take more time for the second-year tackle to recover from the patellar tendon tear he suffered in January, however. The 2025 second-round pick will need at least a few more weeks’ worth of practice before the Bears will feel comfortable moving him back to their starting LT spot, the Chicago Sun-Times’ Patrick Finley notes. Though, Trapilo has come a long way; the Bears had been concerned at one offseason juncture he would miss all of 2026.

Trapilo went down with the patellar tendon tear hours after Panthers LT Ikem Ekwonu suffered the same injury in the wild-card round. Ekwonu is not yet off Carolina’s active/PUP list. The Panthers have a clear plan while Ekwonu recovers, having signed Rasheed Walker from the Packers. The Bears have not settled their Trapilo contingency plan yet. Ben Johnson said (via ESPN.com’s Courtney Cronin) the team is not 100% sold on who will be in the starting lineup against Carolina in Week 1.

Braxton Jones held this position for most of his rookie contract, before being benched midway through last year. The re-signed tackle entered training camp as the favorite, but he has not won the job over Theo Benedet, Kiran Amegadjie and Jedrick Wills yet. That said, Finley places Jones and Benedet as safely on Chicago’s 53-man roster while classifying Amegadjie and Willis as having work to do. Amegadjie is a 2024 third-round pick who spent most of last season on IR, while Wills was a five-year LT starter in Cleveland before a knee injury led to him being out of football last season.

title: Is it fair at this point to question Kyler Gordon? - Windy City Gridiron
description:
Kyler Gordon is entering his fifth season in Chicago.
At this point, with the Bears clearly frustrated, is it time to question Gordon’s motivation to get back on the field?
But Gordon was paid in August of 2025, and since then, not only has he barely played, he’s barely practiced.
Is it fair to question Gordon’s motivations and wonder if he’s lost his drive to play now that he has a contract that guarantees him $31 million?
Only time will tell, but as for now, I’m just wondering if it’s time to question Kyler Gordon?
text:
Over the years as a sports fan, I have certainly questioned a player or two about their desire to get back on the football field. But over the years I’ve learned that’s not a good idea.

I will admit, I originally questioned Jay Cutler in the moment during the NFC Championship game when we had the Caleb Haine experience. In hindsight, that was stupid.

It took me a long time to question Nate Davis. Let’s not forget, the summer Nate Davis arrived in Chicago, his mother died. It’s impossible to know how that’s going to affect someone’s professional life, and to this day, we still really don’t know how that impacted him.

Kyler Gordon is entering his fifth season in Chicago. And while he’s never played a full season, before last year, he never missed more than 4 games in a season. Last year, Gordon missed 14. This year, Gordon basically hasn’t been on the field at all.

If the Bears were coming out and talking about Gordon’s injury and how his rehab is going and a projected timeline, we would be classifying this as an unfortunate injury, but that’s not what the Bears are saying.

Both Ben Johnson and Ryan Poles have been pretty flippant talking about Gordon during the spring and summer and certainly seemed agitated about his lack of progress and lack of participation. They also seem to be missing details about what his status is.

The Bears have plenty of injured players. You don’t hear Johnson or Poles talking about any other injured players like that. We just heard Ben Johnson say that “ALMOST every player” that is injured is trying hard to get back on the field. That certainly seems like a shot at Gordon.

At this point, with the Bears clearly frustrated, is it time to question Gordon’s motivation to get back on the field?

Like I said at the top, questioning an injury with a player is almost always bad business. I think 19 times out of 20 (maybe more), you find out that you didn’t have all the information and the player was more hurt than anyone realized (sometimes coaching staffs included).

But let’s go back to Nate Davis. And now, I am not saying Gordon is Davis. But Davis clearly didn’t want to play football. Davis got through his rookie contract, signed a contract that earned him $20 million guaranteed with the Bears, and at that point, decided to do the bare minimum to fulfil his contract so he could collect his money.

At this point, we know Davis was released in November of 2024, and he hasn’t even sniffed a tryout with another team. Davis is a good enough player that teams would absolutely bring him in for a tryout if he was interested. He clearly is not.

Is that Gordon’s situation? I have a hard time believing that. Gordon has played hard in plenty of football games and has never come across that way. But Gordon was paid in August of 2025, and since then, not only has he barely played, he’s barely practiced.

Ryan Poles is frustrated. Ben Johnson is frustrated. Chicago Bears fans are frustrated. Is it fair to question Gordon’s motivations and wonder if he’s lost his drive to play now that he has a contract that guarantees him $31 million?

We’ve seen more and more players retire at younger ages once they get the guaranteed money from their second contract. Heck, Drew Dalman only got through one of his two guaranteed years before he decided to hang it up.

Has Kyler Gordon quietly quit?

I certainly hope not, and I’m not there yet, but I have to admit, the thought is now creeping into my mind. I don’t like that it has, but it’s almost impossible at this point not to start thinking it’s a possibility.

For now, we wait. We see if Gordon gets on the field in the regular season, and we see how hard he’s playing and how effective he is.

If this dance continues throughout the season, every Bears fan is going to have the same thought. If Gordon gets on the field and plays 12 or 13 games and looks good in the process, we are all going to put this behind us.

To me, I’m starting to wonder if this is similar to the Derrick Rose situation with the Bulls. Rose, post injury, was very honest about how he approached injuries and how he wasn’t willing to punish his body if it meant the possibility that his body breaks down in the future when he’s in his 50s and 60s. That frustrated Bulls fans, but when Rose was on the court, he was 100% committed to being on the court. It was how he approached his recovery that was frustrating.

Is Gordon the same? Only time will tell, but as for now, I’m just wondering if it’s time to question Kyler Gordon?

title: Jets' Chip Trayanum hospitalized with neck injury after early TD in 23-6 preseason loss to Giants
description:
The Jets announced that Trayanum, an undrafted rookie running back from Toledo, was awake, alert and had movement in his extremities.
The 24-year-old native of Akron, Ohio, played a major role on offense early with the Jets (1-2).
The Jets ran on 10 straight plays, including nine by Trayanum, who capped the drive with 1-yard touchdown run.
“Overall, not my best ball,” Klubnik said.
Early in the second quarter, Beckham got behind the coverage and Winston threw a deep pass that appeared on its way to being a 73-yard touchdown.
text:
EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. (AP) — Chip Trayanum was taken to a hospital with a neck injury after earlier running for a touchdown in the New York Jets’ 23-6 preseason loss to the Giants on Friday night.

The Jets announced that Trayanum, an undrafted rookie running back from Toledo, was awake, alert and had movement in his extremities.

“I think he’ll be just fine,” coach Aaron Glenn said after the game. “He’ll be just fine.”

Trayanum saw extended snaps and finished with 38 yards on 12 carries as Glenn and the Giants’ John Harbaugh rested almost all of their projected starters. With 10 seconds remaining before halftime and with the ball deep in their own territory, the Jets opted to hand it off to Trayanum — who was immediately walloped by Trace Ford.

Jets players and coaches remained on the field — many on their knees and praying — as Trayanum was examined in a scary and eerily quiet scene at MetLife Stadium. He was put in a neck brace, strapped to a backboard and loaded onto a cart and driven off the field.

The 24-year-old native of Akron, Ohio, played a major role on offense early with the Jets (1-2).

After Marcelino McCrary-Ball intercepted Jameis Winston — who started in place of Jaxson Dart — on a pass intended for Odell Beckham Jr. that was deflected by Qwan’tez Stiggers, the Jets’ offense hit the ground running.

Literally.

The Jets ran on 10 straight plays, including nine by Trayanum, who capped the drive with 1-yard touchdown run. Rookie quarterback Cade Klubnik, starting in place of Geno Smith, had the other rush on a 6-yard scramble.

Jason Sanders, who won the Jets’ kicker competition this week by beating out Cade York, was wide left on the extra point. He also was short on a 54-yard field-goal attempt.

With the Giants (2-1) driving deep in Jets territory on their next possession, McCrary-Ball punched the ball out of Braxton Berrios’ hands and Stiggers recovered in the end zone for a touchback.

The Jets couldn’t take advantage and went three-and-out. A 16-yard run by Tyrone Tracy and a 23-yard catch by Beckham got the Giants to the 6, and Tracy ran it in to put the Giants up 7-6 with 28 seconds left in the opening quarter.

Klubnik has a so-so showing in his bid to be the Jets’ No. 2 QB

Klubnik, a fourth-round pick, was intercepted early in the second quarter by Zaire Barnes, a sixth-rounder of the Jets in 2023 who signed with the Giants last year. It was Klubnik’s first turnover of the preseason.

He played the entire first half and was 6 of 13 for 59 yards and the INT. He was replaced by Bailey Zappe to start the third quarter.

“Overall, not my best ball,” Klubnik said.

Glenn said Klubnik was “up and down” and declined to declare him the No. 2 quarterback behind Smith.

Beckham almost makes a sparkling play like the OBJ of old

Beckham, possibly looking to secure a roster spot, caught three passes for 53 yards on six targets in the first half. But he nearly had an amazing catch.

Early in the second quarter, Beckham got behind the coverage and Winston threw a deep pass that appeared on its way to being a 73-yard touchdown. But the ball was slightly overthrown and Beckham dived, but it went off his fingertips when he hit the ground.

“I don’t want to say exactly that he’s making it right now or not, what the considerations are, and things can happen,” Harbaugh said. “But I think I would answer the question, yes, I think he has done enough to make an NFL roster, for sure. He’s played well.”

The 33-year-old Beckham, a first-round pick of the Giants in 2014 who played five seasons with the franchise, re-signed with his original team in June. His chances of making the roster improved when Calvin Austin tore the ACL in his right knee earlier this week.

“Super grateful for the opportunity,” Beckham said. “At this point, it’s in God’s hands. I know that I have a good feeling about myself. I feel like there’s ball to be played, plays to be made.”

Haener leads late TD drive for Giants

Jake Haener, fourth on the Giants’ depth chart behind Dart, Winston and Brandon Allen, had a 37-yard touchdown pass to Xavier Gipson in the fourth quarter.

Haener, who spent his first three NFL seasons with New Orleans, signed with the Giants last week.

Zvada wins Giants’ kicking competition

Harbaugh announced that rookie Dominic Zvada won the Giants’ kicker job, beating out Ben Sauls.

Zvada kicked field goals of 23, 53 and 46 yards against the Jets and made both of his extra points.

Injuries

Giants: Tracy left in the second quarter to be evaluated for a concussion, but was cleared to return.

Jets: Glenn said CB Tre Brown was taken to a hospital because of a finger injury. … Edge rusher Joseph Ossai left in the first quarter with a foot injury. … Rookie G Anez Cooper, a sixth-round pick, was ruled out after injuring his right shoulder in the second quarter. … WR Cam Camper was evaluated for a concussion in the second half and cleared. … RB Dominic Richardson injured an elbow in the fourth quarter.

Up next

Giants: Host Dallas in a Sunday night matchup on Sept. 13.

Jets: Take on former coach Robert Saleh and the Titans in Tennessee on Sept. 13.

title: Eagles' Makai Lemon glad to get blunders out of way in preseason - NBC Sports Philadelphia
description:

“Just cleaning up little mistakes really,” Lemon said about the benefit of getting this one out of the way.
“Dropping the ball like that, I’m glad it happened in the preseason so come around September, things like that won’t happen.” After missing the first two preseason games with a hamstring injury, Lemon made his NFL preseason debut against the Bengals on Friday night at the Linc.
They were simply encouraging the rookie throughout his first NFL game action.
As of Friday night, Lemon said his hammy is feeling good.
text:
Makai Lemon got his first taste of NFL game action on Friday night.

And it didn’t go well.

But if the 22-year-old rookie from USC had to struggle at some point, he’s happy those blunders happened in the preseason. He hopes that’s where they’ll stay.

“Just cleaning up little mistakes really,” Lemon said about the benefit of getting this one out of the way. “Dropping the ball like that, I’m glad it happened in the preseason so come around September, things like that won’t happen.”

After missing the first two preseason games with a hamstring injury, Lemon made his NFL preseason debut against the Bengals on Friday night at the Linc. Lemon started the game but wasn’t very productive. He was targeted 5 times and finished with just 3 catches for 3 yards.

Lemon also muffed a punt and had a costly drop that led directly to an interception.

The pass on the INT from Tanner McKee wasn’t perfect. McKee admitted after the game that he needs to keep the ball down. But Lemon wasn’t interested in excuses, even when potential outs were presented to him.

“It’s a drop,” Lemon said. “It hit my hands. It went through my hands. I gotta catch them. You know, learn from it.”

The broadcast of Friday night’s game showed some of Lemon’s veteran teammates chatting with him after some of his mistakes. They were simply encouraging the rookie throughout his first NFL game action.

That meant a lot to him.

“Learn from it and forget about it,” Lemon said about their message to him. “You can’t beat yourself about it, man. Next play mentality, really. Just appreciate the guys having my back. I’m real hard on myself, I’m a perfectionist so when things like that do come about, I just have to forget about it and move on.”

Lemon admitted it’s sometimes difficult for him to let his mistakes go, but said that’s part of being a professional. He needs to learn from his blunders on Friday night, but he can’t dwell on them either. Because the Eagles are going to need him.

During the last week of practice, Lemon returned from injury and was immediately back on the field with the starters as the Eagles’ slot receiver. DeVonta Smith and Dontayvion Wicks are expected begin the season as the team’s outside receivers, but Lemon is going to be in the slot. That’s an important role.

And it seems likely that when the rest of the starters are on the field with Lemon, it’ll make his life easier.

“There's going to be ups and downs for every player,” head coach Nick Sirianni said. “There's going to be good plays, bad plays. Obviously, [Lemon is] going to want that catch back on third down to be able to hang onto that, not cause a turnover that obviously led to points. We've seen some good things throughout his practices where we are feeling good about his development. He's got to continue to develop, a young player and we know we're going to be able to count on him this year.”

In addition to Lemon’s role as a slot receiver, he might also be asked to return punts in 2026. He got one return rep on Friday night and muffed a bouncing punt before eventually corralling it.

Lemon took responsibility for that, saying that punts aren’t always going to be hit right to you. He needs to be ready for bouncing footballs like that when the regular season begins.

But Lemon does enjoy getting chances to return.

“For sure,” he said. “Coaches trust me enough to be out there, so I gotta make sure that I know to do my job to the fullest wherever the ball’s going to be at.”

Lemon missed nine training camp practices and the first two preseason games with a hamstring injury after dealing with a hamstring injury on the same leg in the spring. As of Friday night, Lemon said his hammy is feeling good.

He also said the speed of Friday night’s game didn’t feel any faster than what he has experienced in practice.

Does he feel ready for the regular season opener in just over two weeks?

“I feel real prepared,” Lemon said, “but we still got some time so I got to make sure I lock in each week.”

title: 2026 NFL projected sack leaders: Top 50 pass rushers - ABC7 New York
description:

text:
Myles Garrett broke the single-season sack record last season, but a different edge rusher leads our 2026 sack projections.

That player? The Detroit Lions' Aidan Hutchinson, who our statistical model forecasts to rack up 12.5 sacks this season.

This is the sixth consecutive year we've run our sack forecast for veteran pass rushers based on a statistical model that uses information about a player's past performance and current circumstances to project how many sacks he will record in the upcoming season. The model's inputs include:

Sack totals and rates for each of the past two seasons

Projected snaps, via ESPN's Mike Clay

Pass rush win rate, which uses data from NFL Next Gen Stats

Past sack rates for the quarterbacks on each player's schedule

Team win totals from the betting market

Where a player aligns

Age

Only defensive linemen and edge rushers are included, and rookies are excluded. Also, though we recently upgraded our pass rush win rate metrics, this analysis features the legacy version of that metric. Future years will incorporate the upgrades. These projections often appear low. However, they are a projection of a player's mean outcome in 2026 -- including injuries. If we could guarantee health for every player, everyone's forecast would be much higher.

Now, let's dive into the 2026 projections, looking at the top 10 forecasts, plus a few other notables (including one outside the top 50). There's also a top-50 list below.

Jump to:

Projected top 10 | Full top-50 list

More notable projections to watch

1. Aidan Hutchinson, Detroit Lions

Projected mean 2026 sack total: 12.5

2025 sack total: 14.5

This is the second straight year that Hutchinson leads our sack projections, despite having never actually led the league in sacks. But everything lines up for him to have a huge season.

Two years ago, he had a prolific first five games (7.5 sacks, 35% pass rush win rate) before suffering a season-ending leg injury. Last season, Hutchinson stayed healthy and delivered 14.5 sacks in 17 games. If anything, this projection might be underrating Hutchinson, because while his legacy pass rush win rate was above average, he moved up to fourth among edge rushers in the updated version.

The other big reason Hutchinson's forecast is so strong is playing time. Unlike many pass rushers, Hutchinson rarely comes off the field. He played 91% of his possible defensive snaps last season, a much higher rate than players such as Will Anderson Jr. (66%) or Nik Bonitto (62%).

Hutchinson has two other perks working in his favor, the quality of the Lions' overall team (eighth in ESPN's Football Power Index) and the ease of their schedule (second easiest, according to FPI). That means Detroit should be ahead often, which is when sacks most frequently occur.

2. Micah Parsons, Green Bay Packers

Projected mean 2026 sack total: 11.1

2025 sack total: 12.5

The X factor is how much Parsons will play. Clay has Parsons projected to play 619 snaps this season, slightly down from the 669 he played in 14 games in 2025 -- which indicates a slight increase in snaps per game if Parsons were to come back from his knee injury in Week 6 and play the rest of the season. Still, it's incredible that Parsons is projected to miss a third of the season yet still manages to have the second-best forecast.

How?

If we compare him to Myles Garrett, Parsons had a better pass rush win rate in each of the past two seasons, more sacks per game two years ago, is more than three years younger and is on a team that blitzes more. But if there's one overriding reason Parsons is ranked here, it's the combination of win rates alongside his previous double-digit sack seasons.

Parsons is a master of winning on a down-to-down basis but has never had more than 14 sacks in a season. But that could happen at any moment.

3. Will Anderson Jr., Houston Texans

Projected mean 2026 sack total: 10.5

2025 sack total: 12

Anderson emerged as truly elite in 2025, finishing second in Defensive Player of the Year voting to go along with his 12 sacks. There's no reason to expect a drop-off this season.

Anderson has proved himself the past two seasons in terms of sacks and pass rush win rate, is young and on a relatively good team (the Texans' win total at DraftKings is 9.5, shaded to the over) with a particularly good defense. He and Danielle Hunter (8.7 projected sacks, 12th most) make up arguably the NFL's most fearsome pass rushing duo.

Plus, the Texans get the additional bonus of facing a sack-friendly schedule of quarterbacks that includes games against Lamar Jackson (9.8% sack rate), Justin Herbert (8.8%), Jaxson Dart (8.5%) and Cam Ward (9.4%) twice.

4. Nik Bonitto, Denver Broncos

Projected mean 2026 sack total: 10.3

2025 sack total: 14

Bonitto backed up his breakout 13.5-sack campaign in 2024 with 14 sacks in 2025. This season, he gets the benefit of being part of a Broncos defense that is not only strong overall (with great cornerbacks) but also blitzes at an above-average rate.

If there's one thing holding Bonitto back, it's playing time. Last season, he only played 62% of Denver's defensive snaps and was in only 60% of the time in clear pass-rushing situations. That puts a ceiling on his forecast. In addition, Bonitto is a player we might be overrating based on the use of the legacy win rates, which were higher on him than the updated version released a week ago. Still, this is a mighty strong projection.

5. Myles Garrett, Los Angeles Rams

Projected mean 2026 sack total: 10.1

2025 sack total: 23

Yes, I'm as surprised as you are that Garrett is not No. 1 on this list. Even though I know how the model works, I still thought the NFL-record 23 sacks from last season would be enough to put him over the top. Not quite, it turns out!

There are three primary factors working against Garrett:

1. He is 30 years old

2. The Rams blitzed only 19% of the time last season, the second-lowest rate in the NFL

3. Los Angeles faces a quarterback slate that takes sacks less frequently than average

That's enough to hold back Garrett's projection, even coming off a record season in which he was the NFL's Defensive Player of the Year. And his age is a definite factor. While it's possible Garrett will be the same type of elite player well into his 30s, this model considers the drop-off of some previous edge rushers at this point in their careers.

Do I think having Garrett fifth is underselling him a bit? I do, especially since the model is not considering the possibility of Aaron Donald unretiring and taking some heat off him. But there are real variables that are holding back Garrett's 2026 sack projection.

6. Brian Burns, New York Giants

Projected mean 2026 sack total: 9.7

2025 sack total: 16.5

Burns has always been a very good pass rusher -- and something of a pass rush win rate darling -- and exploded for 16.5 sacks in his second season in New York. And the Giants' pass rush has gotten even deeper.

Those 16.5 sacks are enough to launch Burns, 28, into the top 10. But he has a few things working against him. His forecast is negatively affected by only having 8.5 sacks in 17 games in 2024. And while the Giants have a great pass rush, they aren't expected to be a great team. Middling teams don't play with a lead as often, which means fewer desperate opponents frequently passing to catch up.

7. Nick Bosa, San Francisco 49ers

Projected mean 2026 sack total: 9.4

2025 sack total: 2

This assumes that Bosa is healthy enough to play Week 1, which isn't a guarantee right now. The star edge rusher has been out for most of training camp with soreness and tendinitis as he works his way back from a torn ACL suffered last September.

Despite the injury, Bosa's previous history is enough to include him in the top 10. In 2024, Bosa recorded nine sacks and also ranked fifth in pass rush win rate at edge. And now he's being coordinated by Raheem Morris, whose Falcons team blitzed on 35% of its defensive snaps last season, the second-highest rate in the league.

8. Tuli Tuipulotu, Los Angeles Chargers

Projected mean 2026 sack total: 9.3

2025 sack total: 13

Tuipulotu's upward trajectory continued in a big way in 2025, his third season in the NFL, as he followed up an 8.5-sack 2024 campaign with 13 last season.

Tuipulotu has never been a top win rate player and finished well below average in pass rush win rate last season despite his sack total. That hinders his projection, but doesn't crush it. There are players who consistently record more sacks than their win rates would suggest, and it's possible Tuipulotu is one of them. Still, not winning as frequently on a down-to-down basis caps his upside.

9. Trey Hendrickson, Baltimore Ravens

Projected mean 2026 sack total: 9.2

2025 sack total: 4

Hendrickson had only four sacks in his final season in Cincinnati but accomplished that total in seven games due to injuries. He did record a league-leading 17.5 sacks in 2024, which is much more important for his placement on this list.

He's also a pass rush win rate stalwart -- he ranked second at edge in 2024. That, coupled with his prolific 2024 sack total, overrides Hendrickson's limited sack number last season and his advancing age (he turns 32 in December).

10. Alex Highsmith, Pittsburgh Steelers

Projected mean 2026 sack total: 8.9

2025 sack total: 9.5

Highsmith tops the Steelers' edge trio in sack projections after accumulating 9.5 sacks in 13 games. Similarly, his six sacks in 2024 were accomplished in only 11 games. The model not only evaluates players by their total sacks in each of the previous two seasons, but also their sacks per game, which helps Highsmith.

He is also a relatively strong rush win rate player and faces a favorable slate of quarterbacks. Two games against the Browns likely means facing Deshaun Watson, who had a massive 12.5% sack rate in 2024, Shedeur Sanders (a high 9.1% sack rate in 2025), or a combination of the two. Highsmith will also get two games against Lamar Jackson (9.8%), and faces Cam Ward (8.9%), Tyler Shough (8.3%) and Drake Maye (7.8%), who were sacked at a significantly higher rate than the 6.2% average.

Other notable projections

20. Odafe Oweh, Washington Commanders

Projected mean 2026 sack total: 7.0

2025 sack total: 7.5

Oweh is coming off an interesting season in which he recorded zero sacks in five games with the Ravens, following by 7.5 in 12 with the Chargers after being traded. Which was the real Oweh?

I'd say ... both? Oweh was actually recording a strong pass rush win rate before the trade -- it just didn't result in sacks. The sacks eventually came once he went to Los Angeles and Washington paid big money for Oweh to fill their edge-rushing void.

Will he? To some degree. Oweh has demonstrated an ability to win on a play-to-play level and can deliver sacks. And finishing 20th on this list is solid, even if the 7.0 forecast doesn't feel amazing. But Washington fans should be realistic. Oweh is a good pass rusher, but not a great one. At $24 million per year in today's cap environment, that's essentially what they paid for.

22. Abdul Carter, New York Giants

Projected mean 2026 sack total: 7.0

2025 sack total: 4

This is a bullish forecast for a player coming off a four-sack season -- especially because the model does not explicitly consider draft capital (Carter was the third overall pick in 2025) in its computations.

But what it does see is a young player who had a top-10 pass rush win rate. That's enough to generate a strong number despite being on a below-average team with a defensive coordinator who didn't blitz much last season. I wouldn't be shocked if Carter is in the top 10 of the sack leaderboard come January.

26. Jeffery Simmons, Tennessee Titans

Projected mean 2026 sack total: 6.9

2025 sack total: 11

Simmons is the highest-ranked defensive tackle on this list. And while 6.9 sacks might feel insulting considering how well he played last season, it speaks to how much playing in the interior reduces sack expectations.

But there are other factors keeping Simmons' projection in check. As incredible as he was last season -- he was a first-team All-Pro and finished second in pass rush win rate at defensive tackle -- it was the first year he registered double-digit stats or finished that high in win rate. Plus, being on a bad team will limit his sack opportunities, even if he overcame that last season.

51. Dexter Lawrence II, Cincinnati Bengals

Projected mean 2026 sack total: 5.6

2025 sack total: 0.5

After a down 2025 season, Lawrence was traded to the Bengals from the Giants for the 10th overall pick. What kind of player will the Bengals get -- the Lawrence of a few years ago or who he was last season? The projections are splitting the difference.

Lawrence's sacks fell off last season despite him playing less nose tackle than the previous couple of years. But the projections won't totally quit him because of what he has done in the past. Plus, the Bengals face the easiest schedule in the league this season overall (which helps their predicted win total) and the easiest schedule of quarterbacks in terms of past sack rate.

text:
NEW YORK (AP) — After sitting out more than four months nursing an injured right wrist that caused him to miss the French Open and Wimbledon, Carlos Alcaraz didn’t decide to return for the U.S. Open to be anything less than his Grand Slam-winning self.

“You’re going to see Carlitos playing the way he always has,” Alcaraz said.

The 23-year-old from Spain is set to play his first competitive singles match Monday since getting sidelined by the wrist injury in mid-April. He insists he has not changed anything about his mechanics and expressed confidence about physically feeling great.

“I need competition,” Alcaraz said Friday. “We, my team and me, believe that I’m ready. It wasn’t an easy decision. I just did whatever it took to be ready.”

Alcaraz is the defending champion and favored to go back-to-back, a year after beating Jannik Sinner and overtaking him for the No. 1 ranking. The field this time does not include Sinner, who withdrew because of a right knee injury.

“We are not going see each other for, like, six months now, seven months,” Alcaraz said. “It’s kind of a weird situation, to be honest.”

Alexander Zverev is the top seed in Sinner’s absence. But all eyes are on Alcaraz, who earlier this year won his seventh Grand Slam title by defeating Novak Djokovic in the Australian Open final.

“Everyone is going to be pretty tapped in to see his first match,” 11th-seeded American Frances Tiafoe said. “If he comes back anywhere near his level, it’s tough. Regardless, even if he’s not at his tip-top (shape), you’ve still got to beat him in five (sets).”

Alcaraz opens against Roman Safiullin as he dives right back into best-of-five-set tennis in his return. He did get a chance to shake some rust off by playing a couple of mixed doubles matches with Serena Williams this week, but he knows not getting a full ramp up to the U.S. Open adds another layer of difficulty.

“It’s really challenging,” Alcaraz said. “Probably in terms of preparation and everything, (it) is not the best time.”

But the energy of playing in New York was enough of a draw that he said, “There is no better tournament than the U.S. Open to be back.”

Can he win it off such a long layoff? He knows Roger Federer and Rafael Nadal have done it but does not want to set any expectations.

“I’m not going to set a limit for myself,” Alcaraz said in Spanish. “I don’t want to focus on a specific result. I want to focus on the process we’ve gone through. Just go out there, enjoy it and feel good.”

Zverev, who’s now four years removed from tearing ligaments in his right ankle, was reluctant to compare two very different injuries. But he expects Alcaraz to be formidable as the tournament goes on.

“Wrist is never easy,” Zverev said. “I expect him to be maybe a bit rusty the first or second match, but once he gets through that, I think he’s going to be a contender, for sure, here.”

After dealing with intrusive thoughts during his time away from the sport, Alcaraz is still playing a mental game to not worry too much about the injury. His goals are to get through the U.S. Open healthy and stay away from the fear that creeps into his head.

“I just have to go 100%,” Alcaraz said. “I’ve got to trust my team. I’ve got to trust my people that tell me that it’s going to be fine.”
