Purdy’s ranking reflects a similar theme. A toe injury cost him eight games, but NFL.com’s own writeup noted the 49ers scored 37 or more points in four of their final seven games once he returned healthy -- production that suggests his No. 85 slot undersells what he’s capable of over a full season. Williams, at 38 years old and entering his 15th season on a fresh two-year extension, actually improved slightly from his No. 45 ranking a year ago, extending his run to 13 career Top 100 appearances.

Two notable 49ers were left off the list entirely: defensive end Nick Bosa and wide receiver Mike Evans. Both are working back from significant injuries of their own, and since the rankings are determined by players voting on the previous season’s body of work, missed time appears to have cost both players their usual spots -- Bosa ranked 57th just a year ago, with Evans following at No. 44.

Five players across nearly every phase of the roster -- offensive line, receiving corps, defense, and the backfield -- reinforce just how much talent the 49ers are counting on to return healthy after an injury-plagued 2025 season. With McCaffrey back among the league’s elite and four other proven veterans already accounted for, San Francisco enters the year with as much recognized talent as any roster in football.

text:
Tennessee Titans wide receiver Wan'Dale Robinson has reportedly avoided a concussion after a hard hit during a joint practice with the Chicago Bears on Thursday (August 27). The 25-year-old receiver, who joined the Titans this year after four seasons with the New York Giants, was evaluated following a collision with Bears safety Xavier Woods.

The incident occurred during a team period when Robinson caught a pass from quarterback Cam Ward. According to ESPN's Turron Davenport, Robinson managed to walk into the Titans' facility under his own power, despite the severity of the hit. Titans head coach Robert Saleh described the hit as "cheap," a sentiment echoed by Titans players who defended their teammate.

Titans left guard Peter Skoronski and center Austin Schlottmann confronted Woods immediately after the play. Skoronski stated, "You can't have guys like Wan'Dale going down like that on hits that aren't necessary." The incident sparked a scuffle between the teams, highlighting the tensions often present in joint practices.

Robinson, who signed a four-year, $78 million deal with the Titans, is expected to be a key player for the team this season. His teammate, quarterback Cam Ward, expressed relief that Robinson is doing well, saying, "He's good. I gotta put him in a better situation."

The Titans are set to face the Bears in their preseason finale on Saturday (August 29). The incident has drawn attention to the physical nature of joint practices and the need for player safety.

“That’s when I knew, whatever happens with the injury, with baseball, with whatever, he’s good.

It was meant to represent the same foul line he once hopped over, the one that led to his whole journey.
text:
Erik Tolman was hopped up on painkillers, staring down at a mangled knee that now turned in the wrong direction and a foot that he could no longer feel. After recovering from two elbow surgeries across three years, the Washington Nationals left-hander found himself back in a hospital bed, all because he hopped over the foul line on his way to the mound and landed awkwardly.

He wished for peace. Even more than that, he says with disappointment rather than anger, he wished the nurses had kept their voices down.

The artery that delivered blood to his foot was pinched off. Unable to relocate it while at the field or in the ambulance, doctors weighed options for an extremity that had been without oxygen for quite some time — long enough that the nurses in the corner of the emergency room started to whisper.

They were talking about amputating part of Tolman’s leg.

“I mean,” Tolman said, “my life flashed before my eyes.”

Exactly 1,117 days after Tolman thought he was going to lose his right foot, he brushed it across a big-league mound in Miami, a 27-year-old rookie debuting with a substantial brace over his right stirrup sock.

Doctors eventually reached the artery in time. How close of a call it was, Tolman still isn’t sure.

At the time, all he knew was that he was alone, afraid and in pain. His parents were hundreds of miles away, and he had a torn ACL, LCL, PCL, calf, hamstring and meniscus, as well as a paralyzed foot.

“I was embarrassed,” Tolman said. “I was coming back from two Tommy Johns. I’ve always taken pride in how athletic I was. And then for something like that to happen — I mean, it shook me. It shook me.”

After every hour he had ever played and every pitch he had ever thrown, Tolman did not want to be defined as the 14th-rounder whose career ended because his cleat got caught in the turf.

“It caused me to get focused again,” said Tolman, who hasn’t allowed a run in three outings with the Nationals. “I didn’t want that to be the end of my career. No way. There was no way.”

‘Am I ever going to be able to walk normally again?’

Most of the doctors told Tolman to get real.

This, they stressed, would be an abnormal rehab. Maybe he could play baseball at some level again, but he wouldn’t be a big leaguer. Heck, they first needed to figure out if he could walk.

Three surgeries were spread out across 11 months. He saw specialists who worked on skiers and snowboarders, because that was the closest parallel to his injury. They decompressed the nerve, then repaired the LCL, then reattached the hamstring to the bone, then went back to fix the ACL. To keep Tolman’s foot from drooping, they moved a muscle from the back of his leg to the front. At times, he exercised with a makeshift tourniquet on his leg, which was as painful as it sounds.

And so, for a long stretch, no one talked about baseball.

“He never gave up,” said Nick Thurlow, his physical therapist. “But he was also like … ‘I just want to be able to have a functional life and be able to run with my kids one day.’”

Tolman and RJ Dabovich, a former teammate and fellow rehabber who welcomed him during the recovery process, talked about movies. They listened to music and lightened the mood as Tolman learned how to get his foot working again. He wore a shoe around the house so his drooping foot wouldn’t inadvertently kick things. Tolman occasionally had it out with doctors and trainers, always apologizing or changing his tune in time, knowing a breakthrough was on the other side.

“The plateaus for him were a little more life-altering than, ‘Am I going to be able to throw a baseball?’” Dabovich said. “It was, ‘Am I ever going to be able to walk normally again?’ He didn’t know if the feeling in his foot was ever going to come back all the way.”

He shed tears and talked about the depth of the human spirit. He wondered whether he would ever play again or be the same when he returned. He questioned whether he could love the sport again or if it would love him back. For far too long, he was cooped up in his dark room, unable to do much about it.

One day, he looked out his window and decided to do something about it. A few days later, a drone arrived at their doorstep. Tolman and his mom drove toward nature, and he flew the drone over a lake during sunset as geese waddled by their side.

“He just was so overwhelmed by how beautiful things were,” said Linda Tolman, his mother. “That’s when I knew, whatever happens with the injury, with baseball, with whatever, he’s good. He’s going to find a way to do something that makes him happy.”

That spirit, and the support around him, kept him going. The small wins started compounding. He saw his foot move, then started lifting, then walking. Finally, when he got his custom-made AFO for the first time — a brace that supported his foot and ankle — he ran out into the family’s backyard and started sprinting with a big smile on his face.

It started to click: If he could do all of this after almost losing his leg, why couldn’t he pitch, too?

Toothless, Ursula and ‘nothing but smiles now’

Some families play the alphabet game on a long road trip. Others try to spot as many unique license plates as possible. The Tolmans played “things could always be worse.”

Which is why, after all of this, Tolman still describes himself as fortunate, and does so earnestly. He stood in the Nationals clubhouse on a recent afternoon, trying to remember every friend, family member, coach and doctor who helped him along the way. He insisted that, if he had his journal on him, he would flip through the pages to make sure he named every single one.

To finally figure this out, though, he needed some time alone.

“Even if people say they believe in you,” Tolman said, “it won’t work unless you believe in yourself.”

On New Year’s Day 2025, he made the full commitment. After spending some time with friends and his grandma in California, he set forth on a five-and-a-half-hour drive to Arizona. It was one of the first trips where he was able to drive again. He never reached for the stereo.

Instead, Tolman sat in silence and finally asked himself the hard question: Was this really what he wanted to do?

During the drive, he thought through every possible scenario. What would suck? What would cost a lot of money? He sought joy — and potential career paths — wherever he could find them. He thought about a job that would help him save or change lives. Maybe something in the fire department or police force. His mind then went to the medical field. He poked around to see what it would take to join the Coast Guard.

But virtually every single passion he listed out — something that would give him the same joy that baseball did — had a physical limitation, too. So, he thought, “screw it.”

He would be a big leaguer again.

“Since I made that decision, I feel like I’m much happier in life,” Tolman said. “Nothing but smiles now.”

Those around him would argue he always had it in him. He once showed up an hour late to the SATs and smiled his way beyond the closed door. His family had the big backyard where everyone gathered. This spring, pitching coordinator Sean McGrath started calling him “Toothless,” after the injured, resilient dragon from “How to Train Your Dragon.” (Tolman had the figurine of the dragon with him in Rochester, NY.) While rehabbing at his physical therapist’s house, Tolman ended up playing “Little Mermaids” in the pool with Thurlow’s young kids, taking on the role of Ursula. Even last week, a few minutes after Tolman introduced himself to a staffer and walked away, the staffer offered something along the lines of, “I think that’s the nicest guy I’ve ever met.”

Tolman still can’t move his foot side to side. He still can’t feel the top of his foot, either. He still wears the ankle brace, which was once a mental hurdle but now is simply uncomfortable.

He is here in Washington all the same. He can touch 99 mph from the left side with an even nastier slider and changeup.

No one knows what will happen the first time Tolman is asked to run across the foul line, rather than straight in from the bullpen. In Washington, and in Miami, he never had the chance. The best hint, those around him suggest, came from his first bullpen session during recovery.

After five surgeries and a thousand doubts as to whether he could ever pitch again — a thousand reminders to be “optimistic with a plan,” as his mom puts it — Tolman eyed the mound at the training facility in Arizona. The entire facility stopped what they were doing to watch him throw. Garrett Crochet, Logan Webb and a dozen other big leaguers were giddy to see what might happen.

Someone taped a line on the ground next to the mound. It was meant to represent the same foul line he once hopped over, the one that led to his whole journey.

He stomped on it.

text:
A new report has added to the growing debate of the dangers of head injuries in professional sport with nearly a quarter of all former National Football League (NFL) players who died from 2016 to 2021 having confirmed chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) – a neurodegenerative disease linked to repeated head impacts – at death.

Players whose brains showed the most advanced CTE (stage IV) were also more likely to have symptoms typical of dementia before death, such as memory loss and impaired cognitive function, the study found.

Previous studies have shown that people who experience repetitive head impacts from contact sports, including NFL players, are more likely to develop and die from neurodegenerative disease such as CTE than the general population.

However, CTE can only be confirmed by post-mortem examination, so the extent of CTE among NFL players and its association with symptoms such as dementia has been unclear.

To address this, the researchers studied brain tissue donated to the UNITE brain banks at the Boston University CTE Centre (333 donors) and Mount Sinai (1 donor), and UCSF ADRC brain bank (4 donors) by American football players who died between 2008 and 2021 and had played at least one NFL game after 1949 (the first year plastic helmets were mandatory) to estimate rates of CTE among this group.

They also accessed players’ medical notes for symptoms typical of dementia during life and reviewed medical histories from clinical interviews with family members or other informants to examine the association between advanced stage CTE and dementia.

Study clinicians confirmed dementia cases and cause of death using all available information. Average age at death was 66.5 years.

It found among 1,712 NFL players who died from 2008 to 2021, 338 (19.7%) players’ brains were studied, 315 (93.2%) of whom had a diagnosis of CTE; thus, the possible CTE prevalence at death ranged between 18.5% and 98.7%.

Among those who died from 2016 to 2021, when brain donation was most frequent, the possible CTE prevalence at death ranged between 24.5% and 97.7%.

Among donors, 104 (30.8%) had stage IV CTE, 202 (59.8%) had dementia diagnosed by a study clinician, and 63 (18.6%) had neurodegenerative disease listed as the main cause of death.

Stage IV CTE in donors was associated with symptoms typical of dementia before death, and with a 44% higher prevalence of study clinician diagnosed dementia.

Because this retrospective observational study relied on post-mortem brain donation, causal interpretation requires caution. The researchers acknowledged several limitations, including that not all former NFL players who died during the study window were included and that some informants may have overemphasised or inaccurately recalled symptoms.

However, they said: “Together, these findings indicate that NFL players have a higher prevalence of CTE at death than has been previously shown in multiple community based studies. Furthermore, these data indicate that CTE severity at death is significantly associated with dementia in NFL player brain donors, and that dementia is common in these donors.”

Additional work is needed to further clarify the nature of this relation, particularly in other populations, with high lifetime exposure to repetitive head impacts, they conclude.

“This study provides one of the most informative estimates to date of CTE burden among former NFL players,” the researchers added.

“Above all, existing and emerging evidence on this issue must be regularly shared with past, present, and prospective NFL players, ensuring that consent to play is obtained with knowledge of the potential risks involved and the limitations of the current research evidence,” they concluded.

Thew finding will be viewed with interest in the UK where professional rugby players have expressed concerns about the dangers of concussive head injuries and the long term effects.

title: A thought on all 90 Eagles leaving 2026 training camp - NBC Sports Philadelphia
description:
Here’s a thought on every member of the team at the end of training camp: RB Saquon Barkley: Saquon still looks like Saquon.
LB Zack Baun: We probably don’t talk about Baun enough but the 29-year-old has quietly put together another impressive training camp.
There’s no guarantee that Bell is the long-term replacement for Johnson, but that seems way more likely after this training camp.
He got off to an impressive start in training camp and was clearly ahead of Tanner McKee.
Ultimately, Epenesa had a good training camp and, if nothing else, should be a rotational edge rusher.
text:
After 17 practices this summer, the Eagles officially wrapped up training camp on Wednesday afternoon.

The Eagles will finish their preseason on Friday night when they host the Cincinnati Bengals at the Linc. Then they’ll have until 6 p.m. on Sunday to trim their roster to 53 players.

Here’s a thought on every member of the team at the end of training camp:

RB Saquon Barkley: Saquon still looks like Saquon. He had a bit of a down year in 2025 but he has looked explosive in this new wide-zone scheme and has been able to bust a few long runs. He has also caught some passes out of the backfield, which we could see more of this season in Sean Mannion’s offense.

LB Zack Baun: We probably don’t talk about Baun enough but the 29-year-old has quietly put together another impressive training camp. He has had some splash plays but is always solid. His ability to move sideline to sideline is still very impressive. He covers a lot of ground.

OT Markel Bell: The rookie from Miami had a tremendous training camp. He was able to play both left and right tackle and even filled in for Lane Johnson with the first team when Johnson missed time. Bell is a massive prospect at 6-foot-9 but he moves well for a guy of that size and is powerful enough to erase defensive players. There’s no guarantee that Bell is the long-term replacement for Johnson, but that seems way more likely after this training camp.

CB Jakorian Bennett: The Eagles traded for Bennett last August and he would have had a shot at the roster with a good summer in 2026. But Bennett was buried on the depth chart to start camp and then suffered a knee injury and has missed time.

NFL

DT Uar Bernard: The 7th-round pick from Nigeria is obviously green but has already made great strides as he learns how to play American football. He still looks stiff but that’s to be expected. His raw power definitely stands out and he has worked hard to get this far. He has also become a favorite of his teammates as they follow his journey. He won’t contribute this year but the Eagles should be willing to use a roster spot based on his developable traits.

RB Tank Bigsby: Because Bigsby didn’t get traded to Philadelphia until late August last year, this was our first chance to watch him in practice and Bigsby didn’t disappoint. His practice style is just like his game style: Full bore. Bigsby is an explosive runner who constantly brings juice to the practice field.

DT David Blay: The Eagles signed Blay on Aug. 10 and he has been buried on the depth chart since his arrival without much chance to really stick at a very deep position.

CB Isaiah Bolden: The Eagles added Bolden on Aug. 17, so he doesn’t have a real chance to make the roster. He was in coverage on the 37-yard game-winning touchdown given up to the Patriots in the second preseason game and seemed confused about his coverage responsibilities on the play.

WR Hollywood Brown: After a slower start to camp, the veteran receiver got better as the summer went on. He was still probably outplayed overall by Elijah Moore, but Brown has a proven track record in the NFL and the Eagles did guarantee him $5 million on his one-year deal. He didn’t play in the second preseason game, which seemed like a good sign for his roster stock.

TE Grant Calcaterra: The Eagles brought back Calcaterra on a one-year deal, but he had a pretty quiet training camp before going on the shelf with a back injury. A few years ago, Calcaterra was able to fill in admirably for Dallas Goedert but he probably doesn’t need to be on this roster in 2026.

LB Chance Campbell: Last year, Campbell was a menace on the scout team and spent all year on the Eagles’ practice squad. There’s a chance he could make this year’s roster after a solid training camp despite missing some time with an injury. He’s very clearly a favorite of Vic Fangio, who told reporters to not sleep on Campbell.

LB Jihaad Campbell: This is Year 2 for Campbell and he had a good few weeks. His athleticism is apparent. While he didn’t flash as much as Jeremiah Trotter Jr., Campbell got the first-team reps and will start the season next to Zack Baun in the middle of the defense. Campbell did miss one practice when he went back to Alabama to walk at graduation.

DT Jalen Carter: The day before training camp, the Eagles and Carter agreed to a four-year, $152 million contract extension, making him the highest-paid defensive tackle in the NFL. And Carter immediately showed why. He was disruptive early in this camp and returned in excellent shape. Based on what Vic Fangio said about Carter not being in great shape at the start of 2025, that’s a huge deal. Carter looks ready to solidify himself as one of the best defensive players in the NFL.

DB Michael Carter II: It seems unlikely that Carter will beat out Marcus Epps for a starting safety spot, but Carter has had a splashier training camp with more plays on the ball and at least a couple interceptions. He was also the only guy to play three positions this summer. Carter will be on the 53-man roster as a backup safety and nickel and will be the Eagles’ sixth defensive back on the field when they go to their dime package.

WR Darius Cooper: There’s no doubt that Cooper was one of the stars of this training camp but he didn’t finish as strong as he probably would have liked. He made routine and spectacular catches for most of the summer and outplayed the other receivers in camp. But he still didn’t get many first-team reps. Even when DeVonta Smith and Makai Lemon were out, those first team reps went to Dontayvion Wicks, Hollywood Brown and Elijah Moore.

C Zeke Correll: The Eagles didn’t add Correll until Aug. 21 and he played 16 snaps against the Patriots the very next day. He was called for a false start and an illegal use of hands in that game. But Correll has actually gotten some second-team reps when the Eagles were out of bodies.

WR Britain Covey: The problem is that Covey is still the Eagles’ best option as a punt returner but it seems unlikely he’ll make the initial 53-man roster. Covey has had a fine training camp as a receiver but at this point in his career, it doesn’t seem like the Eagles really view him as a wideout. He’s a return man. And they’ll probably try to get him to the practice squad again.

QB Andy Dalton: I just don’t see it with Dalton. He got off to an impressive start in training camp and was clearly ahead of Tanner McKee. But the 38-year-old has come back to earth since then and just simply doesn’t have the arm talent that McKee does at this stage of his career. Dalton has gotten more time as the No. 2 QB and maybe he really will be the backup. But I think McKee would be the better choice.

DT Jordan Davis: The Eagles and Davis agreed to a three-year extension in March and Davis had a solid training camp. He obviously doesn’t flash as much as Jalen Carter or Moro Ojomo as a pass rusher but he was steady. The biggest key for Davis is that he is clearly in better shape at this stage of his career, which is a big deal for him. Davis hurt his elbow in the public practice and has been wearing a brace on his left arm.

DB Cooper DeJean: The big note for DeJean this training camp is that he split his time between nickel cornerback and safety. DeJean is still going to primarily be a nickel corner but will play safety in the Eagles’ base package. While it’s definitely not easy to play a different position, DeJean looked really smooth at safety. It shouldn’t be an issue and it makes sense to find a way to keep him on the field for every snap. He’ll end up playing 75-80% of his snaps at nickel and the rest at safety.

OG Landon Dickerson: Dickerson has denied a report that he contemplated retirement this offseason, but the 27-year-old has dealt with a ton of injuries dating back to his college years. In this camp, Dickerson was able to stay healthy but did get two rest days. He’s the only player to get rest days in camp. While Dickerson looked OK this summer, his health is obviously something to monitor all season because it’s a big key to the Eagles’ success. It's unclear if we'll see Dickerson return to his peak in 2026.

OLB Arnold Ebiketie: There were some pass rushing flashes from Ebiketie during the summer. He has been battling with A.J. Epenesa for a spot in the edge rusher rotation. Ebiketie has had some NFL success and his spin move is one of the best we’ve seen in a while.

K Jake Elliott: During the Eagles’ practices at their own facility, Elliott made all but one of his kicks in a full-team setting but he struggled more up in New England. Of course, those team field goals are just a fraction of the overall kicks he’s attempted over the last few weeks. Based on his last couple of seasons, there are concerns about Elliott going into the 2026 season, but the Eagles are clearly sticking with him.

DE A.J. Epenesa: At 6-foot-6, 280 pounds, Epenesa is the biggest edge rusher on the team. The big question was how he would fare when asked to drop into coverage. It’s something he had never done before. While that’s never going to be his strength, Epenesa didn’t look completely out of place when he needed to drop in this training camp. In the one preseason game, he got beat about 25 yards downfield but that’s tough duty in a 1-on-1 situation. Ultimately, Epenesa had a good training camp and, if nothing else, should be a rotational edge rusher.

S Marcus Epps: It was a quiet training camp for Epps, which isn’t necessarily a bad thing. He has been competing with Michael Carter II for the starting safety job and Epps has gotten way more first-team reps. In fact, that hasn’t even been a rotation. While Carter has made more plays, Epps brings stability and experience to the back end of the Eagles’ defense. And it’s looking like that will be enough for him to earn the starting gig.

WR Erik Ezukanma: The UFL receiver has had some good moments as a receiver in camp and has even been a returner at times, but doesn’t have much of a chance at a crowded position.

LB Brandon George: The Eagles signed George on Aug. 15 and he ended up playing 14 defensive snaps and 7 special teams snaps that night in the Ravens game. He had three tackles the day he signed. Maybe he’s this year’s Chance Campbell.

TE Dallas Goedert: It was a quieter start to this camp for Goedert, which was a tad unusual. But as the summer went on, Goedert became more and more involved in the offense and again became a favorite target of Jalen Hurts. Goedert was also a threat in the red zone this camp after catching 11 touchdowns in 2025. The red zone package has changed a bit with Sean Mannion in charge of the offense, but Goedert is excited about his role in the red zone this season. We also saw Goedert get utilized as a lead blocker a few times.

WR Danny Gray: There’s no doubt that the former third-round pick from San Francisco has some talent but he has never been able to put it together. Gray missed time with a concussion during this training camp and didn’t flash nearly enough to push for a roster spot.

OLB Jonathan Greenard: Technically, Greenard isn’t even on the 90-man roster because he has been on the Active/PUP list all training camp. The veteran edge rusher injured his pec lifting in the Eagles’ weight room ahead of training camp and hasn’t practiced yet. Vic Fangio has even said he’s concerned that Greenard won’t be ready for the season opener, which is obviously not ideal. The Eagles are going to need him this season.

DB Kapena Gushiken: The defensive back from Ole Miss has been a pleasant surprise this training camp. He played safety and nickel and made some plays on the ball. He has an outside shot to make the roster but if he doesn’t, would be an obvious choice to keep around on the practice squad. The fact that Vic Fangio calls him “Gush” doesn’t hurt; a nickname from the DC is always a good sign.

DT Gabe Hall: Last summer, Hall had a tremendous training camp and ended up making the initial 53-man roster. Things were quieter for Hall in this camp and the position is just too loaded for him to make the team. But he could be a good practice squad candidate again.

OL Myles Hinton: When training camp started, Hinton was getting reps at guard and it seemed like a good sign for his staying power. But then that experiment ended and he was back to repping mostly as a third-team tackle. And it hasn’t been going very well. I was intrigued by Hinton at guard and actually think that could end up being his best position, but we didn’t get to see a ton of it. The former sixth-round pick seems unlikely to make the roster.

OLB Jalyx Hunt: He was the star of training camp. It’s hard to overstate just how dominant Hunt looked over the last few weeks. He did it in Philly and then took the show on the road against the Patriots. That shouldn’t be surprising because he was beating Lane Johnson and Jordan Mailata at home. Hunt is entering Year 3 and seems poised for a huge season in 2026. You can argue that Hunt already had a breakout season in 2025, but he’s poised for even bigger things this year after spending most of his summer in the backfield.

QB Jalen Hurts: It was an uneven training camp for Hurts, but that’s to be expected for a quarterback learning a completely new offense — a style of offense that is very different from what the Eagles have run in previous seasons. Hurts threw way more interceptions in this camp and that’s obviously not ideal, but it’s also not a reason to panic. Hurts has a track record of not being interception-prone in the NFL. The best sign from Hurts this summer was his willingness to try new things in this offense and his trust in Sean Mannion to lead.

OLB Tarron Jackson: The Eagles brought back Jackson on Aug. 10 for another stint. He was drafted in the sixth round by the Eagles out of Coastal Carolina back in 2021 and just keeps coming back for more.

OLB Keyshawn James-Newby: The seventh-round rookie from New Mexico suffered an ankle injury on Day 3 of camp and ended up missing eight full days. That’s a shame because he flashed a bit before he went down and since he’s been back with a great pressure on Day 17. And James-Newby has the profile of someone who would be a good special teams player. But he probably missed too much time to make the roster.

TE E.J. Jenkins: Jenkins first got to Philly back in 2023 and has been fighting to stick ever since. He played in two games last season and has played in 10 total in his career. Jenkins is a huge tight end but had a pretty unspectacular camp.

OT Lane Johnson: The future Hall of Famer missed four days early in camp for non-injury reasons and then returned to announce this is likely his last season. Johnson is 36 years old now and feels the pull of real life, which is understandable. But he is still an excellent player and we saw that in camp. It has been cool to hear Johnson get excited to play in a new scheme in Year 14 of his career.

OT Fred Johnson: Over the past couple of years, Johnson has been an important depth piece for the Eagles with 14 starts. But this year, the Eagles drafted Markel Bell in the third round and it was Bell who actually got more first-team reps this summer. Johnson had some rough moments too. He could still be valuable this season but it seems possible that the rookie might just outright win that swing tackle job.

CB Jonathan Jones: The veteran cornerback finally returned to practice on the last day of training camp after missing eight days with a shoulder injury. But before the injury, it was worth noting that Jones was the next guy up with the first team when Quinyon Mitchell would get a break. The Eagles have an excellent starting trio of cornerbacks but their depth is suspect. That makes Jones a sneaky important player this year.

OG Michael Jordan: The Eagles signed the veteran guard, who has 49 career starts, as some veteran depth. But Jordan was mostly buried on the third team and would occasionally bump up with the twos. He is behind plenty of younger players with more upside.

C Cam Jurgens: The best sign in this camp was that Jurgens looked healthy and ready to go. Jurgens dealt with injuries all of last season but his back was clearly feeling way better this summer. That’s obviously very important, especially with this new offense that will ask Jurgens to reach blocks vertically and laterally.

OL Drew Kendall: We’ve seen a big Year 2 jump from Kendall, who had an excellent training camp. He’s likely the next guy in this season if any of the three interior offensive linemen go down. Coming into camp, the interior line depth was a huge question but Kendall’s performance has done a lot to calm those fears. He got time at center and both guard positions.

OL Willie Lampkin: He’s 5-foot-11 and has been discounted at every step of his football journey, but Lampkin can play. There’s just no denying that Lampkin had a great summer and has earned his spot on the Eagles’ 53-man roster. There were obvious questions about how his size would play in the NFL but he’s been a monster. His leverage and strength have been a positive, not a negative.

TE Cameron Latu: Latu is a versatile player who can play tight end, fullback and is a great special teams contributor. He’s clearly not the best natural tight end but it’ll be interesting to see if the Eagles will value Latu’s other strengths. We didn’t see the Eagles utilize a real fullback for most of camp and Sean Mannion played coy when asked about it earlier this week.

LB Deontae Lawson: There were years where the Eagles would have killed to have a rookie linebacker like Lawson. The UDFA from Alabama had a very good training camp and flashed in the preseason. He’s someone who might have a future in the NFL but the Eagles are stacked at linebacker. He’s behind Zack Baun, Jihaad Campbell, Jeremiah Trotter Jr., Smael Mondon and Chance Campbell. So Lawson probably isn’t going to make the roster but he still has some hope.

WR Makai Lemon: It was a shame that the rookie first-round pick missed so much time in this camp with a hamstring injury. But if you had any questions about what the Eagles think of Lemon, they were answered when he returned. He was immediately put with the first-team offense as the slot receiver in 11 personnel and that will likely be his role when the season begins. We’ve also seen the Eagles find ways to get Lemon involved with some manufactured touches and he’s been the guy in motion more than anyone else since his return. As long as Lemon stays healthy between now and Week 1, he’ll have a role on offense as the third receiver. And he’ll also be in the mix as a potential punt returner.

DB Jaylen Mahoney: The Eagles just signed Mahoney on Aug. 24. He was playing safety to close out camp but is still trying to learn the defense.

OT Jordan Mailata: It’s hard to believe that Mailata is entering Year 6 as a full-time starting left tackle. He’s one of the best in the NFL and had a good summer. But even he was on the losing end of some reps against Jalyx Hunt. That says less about Mailata and more about Hunt.

OL Jake Majors: After spending last year on the practice squad, Majors was a second-team offensive lineman all camp, playing both center and guard. He got off to a rough start in pass protection in this camp but came on stronger toward the end. The problem for Majors is that Drew Kendall and Willie Lampkin are both clearly in front of him on the roster and I think the Eagles are more likely to keep sixth-round draft pick Micah Morris too.

P Braden Mann: One of the underrated moves of the offseason was re-signing Mann in free agency. He had an excellent 2025 season and should be good again this year.

QB Tanner McKee: McKee got off to a slower start in this camp but he clearly got more comfortable in this new offense as camp went on. Based on what we saw, McKee closed the gap on Andy Dalton and then passed him in practice and clearly with the second preseason game.

CB Mac McWilliams: McWilliams had to deal with groin and shoulder injuries that limited him a bit. But McWilliams had some good moments and some bad. Vic Fangio seems to be a fan of McWilliams, who is right on the bubble with roster decisions looming.

RB Jordan Mims: The Eagles just signed Mims on Aug. 24 so we haven’t seen much of him. He’ll likely get a chance to play on Friday night.

LB Smael Mondon Jr.: Like we mentioned earlier, the Eagles are stacked at linebacker in this camp. Mondon had an excellent training camp as a rookie and was quieter in Year 2. But he still figures to be a backup and special teams player in 2026.

WR Elijah Moore: The former second-round pick caught a ton of passes this summer and got a lot of reps with the first-team offense and Jalen Hurts. If this was all based on merit, then Moore would be on the 53-man roster. But it’s possible the Eagles won’t keep him. Moore was getting a ton of first-team reps but that was before Lemon returned from injury. With Lemon healthy again, it might make Moore expendable.

OG Micah Morris: The rookie from Georgia missed a couple practices in early August with a shoulder injury but returned and showed some good signs working with the second- and third-team offenses. Morris is a great athlete who is worth developing. I think he’s on the roster.

S Drew Mukuba: In his second training camp, Mukuba has found the consistency that sometimes was missing from his rookie season before it ended in November with a fractured ankle. The good news is that Mukuba is healthy going into Year 2 and will be a full-time starter.

TE Johnny Mundt: The Eagles used their 12 personnel package a ton during this training camp and Mundt was always the second tight end on the field with Dallas Goedert. While the 31-year-old has never caught 20 passes in a single season, he is a good blocker and knows this system. Maybe the Eagles will still look to add another tight end, but if they don’t, expect Mundt to see the field quite a bit.

DT Moro Ojomo: As he enters his fourth season in the NFL, it’s a contract year for Ojomo, who seems poised to cash in. Ojomo last year cracked the rotation and had the first 6 sacks of his career. He has been even more disruptive this summer and has been beating the Eagles’ first- and second-team offensive lines. If Ojomo has a big season, he will likely leave in free agency on a mega deal. There’s literally $100+ million at stake for Ojomo this year.

OT John Ojukwu: The Eagles seem to like the 27-year-old Ojukwu, who played both tackle and guard in this camp. He has 9 career starts under his belt and might be a good player to stash on the practice squad in case injuries ever hit the Eagles’ OL in 2026.

QB Cole Payton: Payton was fun to watch in this training camp. The fifth-round pick from North Dakota State has a fun play style and wasn’t afraid to let passes rip, even when he probably shouldn’t have. For Payton, it’s part of the learning curve as he enters the NFL to realize that windows are going to close quicker than they did in college. Because of that, Payton threw way too many interceptions. But the Eagles like his aggressiveness as a passer and his ability as a runner. Payton got limited reps in practices but the fact that he got reps at all as the fourth-string QB is telling. The Eagles are going to want to develop him. As for the possibility of using him in other roles? We just didn’t see that at all this summer.

RB Dameon Pierce: The former Houston Texans running back got off to a nice start in this camp and it looked like he was going to push Will Shipley for that third running back spot. But Pierce suffered a hamstring injury and fell behind. If the Eagles keep four running backs, he has an outside shot to make the roster. But it’s more likely he won’t be on the team.

S Maximus Pulley: Aside from having a tremendous name, the UDFA from Wofford had some flashy moments in this camp playing mostly as a third-team safety. Pulley has some ball skills and we saw him make some plays on the ball over the last few weeks. I’d have fellow UDFA Kapena Gushiken ahead of him but I think both are worth keeping around on the practice squad.

OLB Jose Ramirez: Ramirez was a sixth-round pick out of Eastern Michigan back in 2023 to the Buccaneers before he went to the CFL to play for the Hamilton Tiger-Cats. Ramirez showed some flashes, especially in that second preseason game, but there’s just not a spot for him.

CB Kelee Ringo: It was another uneven training camp for Ringo. Last year, Ringo had a real shot to win a starting job and couldn’t capitalize. This year, he’s fighting just to make the roster and we saw more of the same. We’ve seen him make some big plays like that INT in the first preseason game. But he’s still too inconsistent and too handsy in coverage. If he makes this roster, it’ll be on the strength of his special teams ability. Perhaps he could be a last-second trade candidate.

DT Ty Robinson: Robinson is a perfect example of why you can’t write players off early in camp. Robinson was buried on the depth chart with the developmental guys and wasn’t showing any signs of life. But then something clicked. Robinson has been a completely different guy the last few weeks and has shown up big-time in the preseason games. Not only has Robinson solidified his spot on the roster, but there’s a legitimate chance he can push for playing time in Year 2.

S Andre’ Sam: For most of the summer, Sam was running with the second-team defense at safety but never got involved in the competition for the starting job. Sam has been solid but the Eagles may have already seen him reach his ceiling.

RB Will Shipley: With Tank Bigsby on the roster, Shipley is clearly the third running back on this team. But Shipley had a good summer, especially in the preseason. He ran very hard against the Patriots last week and turned some heads. Shipley won’t get many chances on offense this year but will be a kick returner and major special teams contributor.

TE Stone Smartt: Smartt’s best play of camp came on Day 17 when he caught a slant in stride from Andy Dalton. But it was an otherwise unspectacular few weeks for the former Jets tight end.

WR DeVonta Smith: The Eagles were without Smith for a good portion of this training camp as he healed from a hamstring injury but they’re very excited to see him take over as their WR1. A.J. Brown was a great player in Philly but his absence will open the door for Smith to have a huge season in an expanded role. When he has been on the field, we’ve seen how good Smith can be. What really stood out this summer was his ability to bring in contested catches against some really good cornerbacks. Smith should shine in Sean Mannion’s offense.

OLB Nolan Smith Jr.: Because Jalyx Hunt was the star of training camp, Smith was in his shadow a bit. But Smith is going to be an important player this season, especially because we don’t know when Jonathan Greenard will return from his pec injury. Smith has been a starter all camp and has been very solid. He has had some really good rushes — an inside win against Lane Johnson really stands out — and has been as solid as ever setting the edge. Smith is healthy right now and that’s a big deal after a disappointing year in 2025.

RB Carson Steele: We didn’t see the Eagles use the fullback position very much in camp and that could really hurt Steele’s chances of sticking. For the most part, Steele lined up as a running back. He really shined in the second preseason game with over 100 scrimmage yards and a couple incredible hurdles. Steele probably passed Dameon Pierce in the pecking order and could be the fourth running back if the Eagles keep four.

OG Tyler Steen: It’s a big season for Steen because he enters the fourth and final year of his rookie contract. He was probably under-appreciated last season because Steen was solid. He was just as steady in this camp and looks like a good fit for this new run scheme. Because the futures of Landon Dickerson and Lane Johnson are very much in question, there’s a path where the Eagles extend Steen after this season.

TE Eli Stowers: There’s no sugarcoating this one. It was a rough training camp for the second-round pick from Vanderbilt. That doesn’t mean he’s a bust; that doesn’t mean he won’t develop. But it’s clear that Stowers isn’t going to be ready to contribute early in his rookie season. Stowers just didn’t flash much at all, which is a bit surprising given his college ability as a pass-catcher. We all knew he would need time to develop as a blocker, but it’s more concerning he wasn’t able to make plays as a receiver. Stowers now has a hamstring injury and the Eagles will have to decide to either keep him on the 53 or put him on IR. If Stowers is on the roster, it’s hard to imagine him having a role early in the season.

CB Ambry Thomas: Thomas is a 26-year-old former third-round pick from San Francisco who hasn’t played in a regular season game since 2023. I give him credit for sticking with it but he didn’t have a very good training camp and won’t make the roster. The lasting memory of Thomas came on Day 17 of camp when he got called for a DPI and wouldn’t stop yelling at the ref.

WR Samori Toure: Toure, 28, is a veteran who was drafted by the Packers in 2022. He has played in 23 career games but was buried on the depth chart in this camp and didn’t really stand out.

LB Jeremiah Trotter Jr.: There’s no doubt that Trotter was one of the stars of the summer. The problem is that Zack Baun and Jihaad Campbell are entrenched as starters. But Trotter can play and could very well start for some teams around the league. The thing that stands out about Trotter most are his instincts in the run game. He’s always in the right spot in a hurry and stuffing the run. He has also shown ability as a blitzer. Trot was good enough in camp that Vic Fangio might try to find a way to get him on the field in some sort of limited role. If not, Trotter will be a valuable backup.

LS Rocco Underwood: The Eagles needed a new long snapper, so they signed Underwood out of Florida. If the team doesn’t feel comfortable with Underwood, they’ll have to find his replacement elsewhere.

CB Shaun Wade: Wade was drafted by the Ravens way back in 2021 and most recently played in the UFL. He forced fumbles in back-to-back preseason games and you love to see that tenacity, but he’s a long shot to make the roster.

WR Tahj Washington: The Eagles just added the 2024 seventh-round pick on Thursday. Washington (5-10, 174) was teammates with Makai Lemon at USC in 2023. He played in 6 games with the Dolphins last season.

WR Quez Watkins: During this camp, Watkins definitely had some ups and downs but at times showed off that 4.35 speed that the Eagles loved when they drafted him back in 2020. He hasn’t played in a regular season game since 2023 and isn’t expected to make this roster.

OLB Joshua Weru: While Uar Bernard has gotten the headlines as a seventh-round pick, Weru is the IPP player who looks way closer to actually be a contributor. Weru was widely considered to be the second-best IPP prospect and he is plenty athletic too. Perhaps his rugby background has helped Weru learn quickly because he has flashed in practices and in games. Heck, he got a sack against the Patriots in the second preseason game. Weru has been good enough that the Eagles have a tough roster decision. They have invested time and effort to help Weru develop and, even though he’s unlikely to contribute this year, they won’t want to risk losing him on waivers. But can they really afford to keep two players who just learned how to play football on their 53-man roster?

WR Dontayvion Wicks: Of all the receivers in this training camp, Wicks was the most consistent with DeVonta Smith missing time. The former Packer clearly built a rapport with Jalen Hurts and his understanding of this scheme likely helped him get ahead. Wicks is so quick in and out of his breaks and can win very quickly at the line of scrimmage. Not only was he consistent in camp, but he also made some spectacular plays. He’s going to go into the season as the Eagles’ WR2.

OT Cameron Williams: A sixth-round pick last year out of Texas, the Eagles have been developing Williams but he was mostly the third-team right tackle in this camp. He did get some reps with the twos. Roster spots are going to be tougher to find on the OL this year and because of that, Williams is unlikely to make the team.

DT Zion Wilson: Wilson has a unique backstory. The NCAA denied his waiver for a sixth year of eligibility in June so he then signed with the Eagles as a UDFA. Wilson is an undersized DT but he wins with leverage and is very tough. The Eagles are just too deep at the position right now.

S Cole Wisniewski: The seventh-round pick from Texas Tech just missed too much time in training camp, first with a hamstring injury and then with a concussion. The concussion against the Patriots in the preseason was a tough break. Had Wisniewski returned from that hamstring injury and had a good final week of camp, I think he could have made the roster because the Eagles don’t have much depth there. But because we barely saw him this summer, that’s a tougher sell.

CB Riq Woolen: After he was the star of spring practices, Woolen just didn’t see many passes go his way early in camp so he had to stay patient. In the first joint practice in New England, Woolen had a rough day, losing to A.J. Brown a few times. But he rebounded on Day 2 and has been making plays ever since. He really showed everyone what he can do in the public practice, when he had two interceptions. One of those INTs was a 75-yard pick-6.

text:
Explosive plays in the NFL might lack a common source or even a universal definition. But it's clear that they remain near the top of every play-caller's wish list.

The exact yardage cutoffs – typically 10-12 for runs and 16-20 for passes – used to measure chunk gains can vary between sources. What's clear, however, is that those big plays remain one of the most effective ways to supercharge an offense that otherwise might have to rely on unwavering precision throughout long drives. And after the Seattle Seahawks and New England Patriots rode their heightened offensive explosiveness all the way to Super Bowl 60, several more aspiring contenders are surely looking to follow the same path to prosperity this season.

But while explosive plays might once have been synonymous with throwing the ball deep downfield, that's not necessarily the case in the NFL's ever-shifting landscape. As several attacks tilt toward heavier personnel and higher run rates, many teams could become more electric by rooting themselves in the ground game.

With that in mind, here are five offenses trending toward being more explosive this fall than they were last season:

Los Angeles Chargers

There might not be a more stark case of year-to-year schematic whiplash than the Chargers pivoting from a Greg Roman-orchestrated offense to a Mike McDaniel-helmed one.

In splitting with one of his longtime trusted assistants in Roman, Jim Harbaugh acknowledged a need for a "fresh start." Just a few months into his tenure, McDaniel is already reshaping the attack, kicking everyone from the once-plodding attack into high gear.

"Yeah, I think he's just going to set us up for a lot more explosives," wide receiver Ladd McConkey said in an NFL Network interview earlier in August. "He's going to get the run game, pass game going. They're going to marry off each other. So I'm super excited about that."

For Justin Herbert, McDaniel's approach has meant prioritizing getting the ball out quicker than he did previously, with the quarterback adjusting his footwork during that offseason to facilitate more yards-after-catch opportunities. The run game, however, might be where things really take off. Though the Chargers ripped off 14 carries of 20-plus yards last year, McDaniel coaxed 16 such gains out of a substantially worse-positioned Miami Dolphins roster. Peppering in plenty of misdirection and pre-snap motion could fully unleash Omarion Hampton and Keaton Mitchell, both of whom have proven fully capable of going the distance when given a crease.

A major problem could be brewing up front, however. One year after season-ending injuries to bookend offensive tackles Rashawn Slater and Joe Alt cratered the Bolts' attack, Los Angeles is looking significantly vulnerable on the interior line. Center Tyler Biadasz was signed as a steadying force, but his season-ending knee injury in training camp prompted second-round rookie Jake Slaughter to shift over from a five-way competition for the starting left guard spot. In a division that features interior game-wreckers in Chris Jones and Zach Allen, the Chargers could see a good number of potentially explosive plays defused if the line gives way.

Kansas City Chiefs

For a team intent on reclaiming some semblance of its bygone explosiveness, bringing back Eric Bieniemy as offensive coordinator was a fitting move.

Bieniemy's previous stint in the role coincided with the franchise's offensive peak from 2018-22, a stretch in which it flummoxed opponents by stretching the field and never ranking worse than sixth in scoring or yards per game. With the offense becoming more methodical in the three years since his departure, generating more big plays has been an annual offseason rallying cry for Kansas City. After last season's 6-11 unraveling, however, it might now be a full-on mandate.

The days of Patrick Mahomes routinely ripping passes over the top of a defense likely won't return, with the Chiefs' subpar receiving corps and opponents' rampant use of two-high shells continuing to significantly box in the aerial attack. Yet the addition of running back Kenneth Walker III might prove transformative for the group.

After years of declining returns from the team's running backs, the Chiefs' ground game finally bottomed out last season. Kansas City only had a perfunctory presence operating from under center, with the team's intentions largely telegraphed. And with a league-low three carries of 20-plus yards on the season, and only one coming from a running back, Mahomes was left to shoulder an even more disproportionate burden as both a runner and overall offensive catalyst.

It's little wonder, then, that the Chiefs were drawn to Walker. The Super Bowl 60 MVP powered a Seahawks attack dependent on big plays with his breakaway speed. Still only 25 and having never logged more than 228 carries in a season, Walker can take on a more sizable role than he's accustomed to and still make Kansas City more dynamic.

Mixing in the occasional long run could alleviate plenty of difficulties for Mahomes. The lack of a consistent threat took a heavy toll on the offense's third-down efficiency, with Kansas City seeing its conversion rate (37.44%) plummet to 22nd in the NFL in 2025 after annually ranking near the top in the previous seven seasons. Walker also figures to hold a prominent role in reviving the screen game and play-action looks, two areas in which the Chiefs were formerly the league's standard-setters but have since fallen off considerably.

Minnesota Vikings

In moving quickly to wrap up their quarterback competition and name Kyler Murray their starter, the Vikings reaffirmed their dedication to chart a new course after losing their way last season with J.J. McCarthy at the helm.

Will the explosive plays filter through as easily as they did in 2024, when Sam Darnold ignited the group to the second-most passes of 20-plus yards (64)? That will be a tough bar for Murray, who's been waylaid by injuries for two of the last three seasons, to clear. Both the dual-threat quarterback and Kevin O'Connell likely still have significant work to do to close the chasm between their respective schematic comfort zones, and Murray might no longer be the out-of-structure virtuoso that he was in his athletic prime.

Then again, he might not need to be. O'Connell clearly has abundant faith in a system that's proven prolific when left to even a capable triggerman. After McCarthy so often squandered opportunities for Justin Jefferson and Jordan Addison by being either late or errant with his throws, a boost in precision could allow Minnesota's pass catchers to flourish with strikes to the sidelines.

The Vikings' skill-position players should also have more time and room to operate after last year's starting offensive line played just 83 snaps together amid widespread injuries. And while the revamped run game remains a work in progress through uneven summer performances, Jordan Mason could rip off more chunk gains as new assistant head coach Frank Smith ushers in more wide-zone looks that suit the running back's style of play.

New Orleans Saints

For most of Kellen Moore's first year as a head coach, his up-tempo attack couldn't seem to find a rhythm. Not only were the Saints hampered by a run game that averaged the second-fewest yards per carry (3.7) of any team, but the passing attack posted the second-fewest 20-yard connections of any offense.

But things looked decidedly on the upswing by the end of the season. During New Orleans' 4-1 finishing stretch, the shorthanded offense averaged 24.8 points per game – nearly a full touchdown better than the team's season-long mark. A good deal of the progress traces back to the installation of Tyler Shough, the eventual NFL Offensive Rookie of the Year runner-up, as the starting quarterback near midseason. Six of the Saints' eight offensive touchdowns spanning 20 yards or more came after he took over for Spencer Rattler behind center.

With running back Travis Etienne Jr. and offensive guard David Edwards signing in the offseason, New Orleans should be more dangerous in almost every phase. The new backfield timeshare between Etienne and Alvin Kamara offers some much-needed staying power after the latter ball carrier averaged a career-low 4.0 yards per touch last season. Having any consistent presence in the ground game could open up additional downfield opportunities for Shough. The selections of first-rounder Jordyn Tyson, fourth-rounder Bryce Lance and sixth-rounder Barion Brown reflect the team's commitment to establishing vertical threats beyond go-to target Chris Olave.

Any progress on this front might be slow to materialize, though. The offense might not be at full strength until well into September as Tyson (hamstring) and Kamara (medial collateral ligament sprain) recover from their respective injuries.

Denver Broncos

Excitement over preseason returns should always be tempered. Nevertheless, the Broncos' early showings offered a tantalizing preview of how Denver might introduce a long-absent facet.

Against the Green Bay Packers in the second week of the exhibition slate, Nix found offseason trade acquisition Jaylen Waddle down the seam for a 35-yard catch-and-run. Three plays later, Nix connected with second-year running back RJ Harvey on a wheel route for a 21-yard touchdown.

That spark was distinct for Denver that returned the core of last year's AFC championship game group, but still is in search of the next level. Through his first two years as a starter, Nix has kept the Broncos squarely in the middle of the pack in most offensive statistical categories. But the drives have often been methodical marches, with few figures breaking through the pervasive sense of stagnation.

Enter Waddle, who remains one of the league's premier speed merchants entering his sixth season. First-year offensive coordinator and play-caller Davis Webb is so enchanted with the dynamic target that he said Waddle will "play everywhere except the offensive line." Creative usage will surely maximize the receiver's output and allow him to create mismatches as a flyweight version of Sean Payton's beloved "joker" role. But his greatest dividends might come in the intermediate and deep middle of the field, areas where Nix still has considerable room for growth.

If Denver can more consistently keep defenses off balance and maintain a steady rushing attack led by J.K. Dobbins, a breakthrough is entirely within reach.

text:
The Buffalo Bills faced the Pittsburgh Steelers in their final preseason game on Thursday night at Highmark Stadium. Many starters rested for both teams, but some did so not for rest, but because of injury.

Bills wide receiver Keon Coleman has been dealing with a foot/toe injury that he suffered in the first preseason game against the Carolina Panthers on Aug. 15.

Advertisement

Coleman has worn a walking boot since the injury, and reporters saw him in it last Saturday when the Bills faced the Cleveland Browns at Huntington Bank Field. But the Bills got some good news on Thursday.

13 WHAM's sports reporter Dan Fetes posted a video on X of Coleman walking onto the field for the game against the Steelers. He wore a long-sleeve shirt and shorts, and there was no boot in sight; instead, he wore two slip-on sandals.

Coleman Has to Have a Good Performance This Season

Coleman is heading into his third NFL season, and he has to make it his best year yet. He has played in 26 games and has recorded 67 receptions for 960 yards and eight scores.

Advertisement

The 6-foot-3 wide receiver missed four games in his rookie season due to a chipped bone in his wrist, and then he missed four games last season because former head coach Sean McDermott listed him as a healthy scratch a few times.

Coleman was late to a meeting before a Week 11 game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. McDermott was not happy, which led him to list Coleman inactive for the game.

"You grow from it, we can move forward. You don't grow from it, it's hard to move forward," McDermott said in November, via Pro Football Talk's Myles Simmons. "So, ultimately, it comes down to developing trust and that trust that your teammates have in you. And that trust builds through repetition and consistency."

Joe Brady Becoming the Bills Head Coach Is a Great Thing for Coleman

The best thing for Coleman was that the Bills decided to move on from McDermott this offseason and make offensive coordinator Joe Brady head coach, giving Coleman a fresh start.

Advertisement

"I made sure once I got the job to let him know, he's going to be here, he's going to be a part of our offense," Brady said in May, via the team's website. "I'm excited about him progressing in this offense and getting with Josh (Allen) and doing those things… I love the work ethic, love how he's kind of been doing it right now."

This is likely Coleman's last chance with the Bills. If he doesn't turn things around this season, there is a good chance Buffalo will look to move on from him after the season. However, one factor that could keep him around for another year is that he will be heading into the final season of his rookie deal, making him relatively inexpensive.

Since the Bills did not select Coleman in the first round, he is not eligible for a fifth-year option. The Bills would have had to pick it up this offseason for him to have a fifth-year option in 2028, but that is only available for first-round picks.

title: 49ers 53-man roster projection: Injuries cloud the picture at OL, LB and CB - The Athletic

text:
LAS VEGAS — Sometimes scores can be misleading. The San Francisco 49ers and Las Vegas Raiders’ tie at 12 at the two-minute warning in Thursday night’s preseason finale was not.

Eddy Piñeiro, who made a 59-yard attempt earlier, kicked a 51-yard field goal for the lead and a 54-yarder as insurance, giving him six field goals in the 18-12 win, but the 49ers were already content to walk away from the boring affair with only one more injured 53-man-roster player than they had coming in: rookie cornerback Ephesians Prysock, who left in the first quarter with a sprained shoulder.

There wasn’t much to be gained in the preseason finale, as only a couple of the 49ers’ potential starters played against the Raiders.

Keion White used a swim move for a sack and was all over the field in a good test, as the Raiders played their offensive starters. Fourth-round rookie Carver Willis, who might be the opening-day starter at left guard by default, was up and down like the rest of the offensive line. The 49ers ran for 91 yards on 15 carries in the first half, but the line did get stuffed twice in short yardage, and the passing game never got going, as Mac Jones and Adrian Martinez combined for 137 yards passing (only 42 yards in the first half).

Niners coach Kyle Shanahan smiled when asked whether any players stood out to him.

“Um, I mean, yeah, there are a few guys,” he said. “I have no problem with praising people, but people in this league get paid a lot of money to read everything we say and evaluate decisions over these next three days based off of practice squads and depth charts and stuff. So I got to be pretty careful with that.”

With the preseason complete, we’ve tag-teamed the final projection for the 49ers’ roster ahead of Sunday’s 3 p.m. PT cutdown deadline, with Vic Tafur handling the offense and Matt Barrows the defense.

Notes: The projection includes three players going to injured reserve with a designation to return (and mentions others who could be IR candidates). Only two players can be given that designation before the cutdown deadline, which could mean additional transactions Monday. Rookies in italics.

Offense (26)

Quarterback (2): Brock Purdy, Mac Jones

Injured reserve: Kurtis Rourke

Cut: Adrian Martinez

Rourke has three broken ribs, which actually gives the 49ers some flexibility, as they would have had to carry three quarterbacks on the roster to keep him, the potential backup in 2027 if Jones leaves to pursue a starting job next offseason. Putting him on short-term IR would rule him out for at least four weeks without taking up a roster spot.

Jones has been a little erratic this preseason and training camp, but he was great last season, winning five of eight starts, and a case could be made the 49ers have the best quarterbacks group in the NFL.

Barrows’ counterpoint: This scenario would leave the 49ers with only two quarterbacks available early on, unless they got Martinez on the practice squad and elevate him for games. That’s certainly possible, though they can elevate only two players per week and might need to use those spots elsewhere. Also, they can elevate Martinez only three times before he would have to be signed to the 53-man roster to be eligible for another game.

Running back (4): Christian McCaffrey, Kaelon Black, Jordan James, Kyle Juszczyk (fullback)

PUP: Isaac Guerendo

Cut: Sincere McCormick, Khalil Herbert

The top three running backs all missed time during training camp, but they’re all ramping up and look very good. James had a 20-yard catch-and-run on a screen and a 17-yard bulldozing run Thursday night. Black, who had a 14-yard run, returned to camp before James and seems to have a firm hold on the No. 2 job, thanks to how hard he hits the hole, good vision and underrated hands.

Wide receiver (6): Mike Evans, Deebo Samuel, De’Zhaun Stribling, Demarcus Robinson, Jordan Watkins, Jacob Cowing

Injured reserve: Christian Kirk

Cut: KhaDarel Hodge, Will Pauling, Wesley Grimes, Malik Turner, Trenton Irwin

Cowing was firmly on the bubble until that touchdown on a punt return last week, and he should send some steaks to the Los Angeles Chargers’ punter. If JK Scott made any kind of effort to tackle Cowing, it would have been a ho-hum 30-yard return for an injury-plagued receiver. Cowing is now battling a groin injury.

Kirk’s calf injury on the first day of camp lingered, and if he goes on IR, that would give Cowing and Watkins — who had four catches for 64 yards and three carries for 19 yards Thursday night — at least another four weeks to make an impression. Robinson seems to have moved past those two because of Purdy’s trust in the vet.

Tight end (3): George Kittle, Jake Tonges, Luke Farrell

Cut: Brayden Willis, Khalil Dinkins, Hayden Rucci

Worst-case scenario, Kittle will be back from his Achilles injury for Week 2 and a three-game homestand. Best case, he’ll give the Los Angeles Rams something to worry about in Australia. The 49ers won’t rush him because they believe in Tonges — he scored the winning touchdown in the season opener in Seattle last year, and Shanahan said he has improved from last season. Willis turned some heads in early August, as he always does, but ran out of steam again.

Offensive line (11): LT Trent Williams, LG Carver Willis, C Jake Brendel, RG Dominick Puni, RT Colton McKivitz, OT Austen Pleasants, G Robert Jones, G Connor Colby, OT Vederian Lowe, OT Enrique Cruz Jr., C Brett Toth

Cut: Brandon Parker, Nick Zakelj, Drake Nugent, Isaac Alarcon, Doug Kramer Jr.

Shanahan said after the game Willis is making a strong push to win the left guard job, and the 49ers hope to have that decided when they return to practice Monday.

A quick tip of the cap to ninth-year vet Parker, who had a great day in one-on-ones in practice Tuesday and will likely be available for the 49ers’ practice squad again. He could even make the roster, as Lowe’s ankle injury is lingering a month later.

Why keep 11 O-linemen? Several are dealing with injuries (including Puni with lingering concussion issues), and the 49ers — a contending team — have to stand firm with the decision to hold a spot for a raw fifth-round rookie (Cruz) who is a year or two away from being ready to play in a regular-season game.

Barrows’ counterpoint: Lowe could begin the season on injured reserve, which would put Pleasants in the swing tackle role he had last year and free up another roster spot. Toth’s lingering concussion symptoms, meanwhile, create concern at backup center. If he can’t play in Australia — or make the 16-hour plane trip — the 49ers would have to think about having Nugent or Kramer in uniform in Week 1. Perhaps Nugent will land on the practice squad and get elevated against the Rams.

Defense (24)

Defensive line (9): DE Nick Bosa, DT Osa Odighizuwa, DT Alfred Collins, DE Romello Height, DE Keion White, DE Sam Okuayinonu, DT CJ West, DT Gracen Halton, DT James Thompson Jr.

PUP: Mykel Williams

Cut: DT Sebastian Valdez, DT Bryson Eason, DT Evan Anderson, DE Ogbo Okoronkwo, DE Quinton Bell, DE Viliami Fehoko Jr., DE Jah Joyner

Thompson, an undrafted rookie, has arguably outplayed all the defensive linemen from this year’s rookie class and last year’s as well. He’s certainly been the healthiest. He, Eason and Valdez have been resilient since the spring, and the 49ers will try to get that group onto the active roster or practice squad.

The team also could stand to stash a defensive end — Okoronkwo? — on the practice squad and elevate him for games early on while Williams rounds into form. Starting the season on PUP means Williams must miss the first four games, but he could rejoin practice after two weeks.

Tafur’s counterpoint: I think the 49ers would be happy with any combination of Thompson, Eason and Valdez on the practice squad, which is why I think they’ll go with only eight D-linemen or with Okoronkwo as the ninth.

Linebacker (6): Fred Warner, Dre Greenlaw, Jaden Dugger, Nick Martin, Garret Wallow, Luke Gifford

Cut: Tatum Bethune, Deion Jones, Larry Worth III, Jalen Graham

Gifford or Bethune? Yes, Bethune played well as the backup middle linebacker last year while Gifford — who had a concussion in the spring and a hamstring issue in the summer — has largely been absent. Still, Gifford made the Pro Bowl last year as a special teamer, and coordinator Brant Boyer will likely go to bat for him as cutdown day approaches. Wallow, meanwhile, might have displaced Bethune, despite his interception in Las Vegas on Thursday night, as the backup middle linebacker.

Not only will Dugger make the 53-man squad, but there’s a good chance he’ll start against the Rams on Sept. 10. He’s their best bet as the third linebacker — and tight end stopper — next to Warner and Greenlaw.

Perhaps the 49ers will try to get newcomer Jones onto the practice squad as Greenlaw insurance. Greenlaw, after all, has started just nine games in the past two seasons. Worth, meanwhile, is a no-brainer practice squad candidate. He’s long (his 33 1/8-inch arms forced a high throw on Bethune’s pick Thursday), lean and versatile, just like Dugger.

Tafur’s counterpoint: I wonder whether Wallow and Bethune will both make it. When asked after the game why Wallow wasn’t suited up, Shanahan referenced back spasms but added Wallow has had “a helluva camp.” Plus, I am not sure how soon they’ll plug Dugger in. He had a missed tackle and a QB pressure Thursday and is still pretty raw.

Cornerback (5): Deommodore Lenoir, Renardo Green, Upton Stout, Jack Jones, Ephesians Prysock

Injured reserve: Nate Hobbs

Cut: Darrell Luter Jr., Eli Apple, Jakob Robinson

Luter has technically been the team’s No. 4 outside cornerback with Prysock in the No. 5 spot. Prysock left Thursday’s game with an AC joint (shoulder) sprain, and his status will likely hinge on the severity of that injury. If he’s not expected to miss much time, the 49ers would go with the big-bodied rookie over Luter, who is in the final year of his rookie contract. The hamstring injury Green suffered last week could also make this spot tricky.

Meanwhile, Jones literally gets his hands on at least one pass per outing — including Thursday — and ought to be the first player off the bench if Green or Lenoir has to come out. Robinson is a nickel specialist who should be back on the practice squad.

Safety (4): Ji’Ayir Brown, Marques Sigle, Malik Mustapha, Siran Neal

Cut: Ashtyn Davis, Jalen Stroman, Patrick McMorris

Mustapha appears close to returning from a hamstring strain suffered early in training camp. If there’s a hiccup, he could go on injured reserve, and Davis would likely make the 53-man roster.

Special teams (3)

PK Eddy Piñeiro, P Corliss Waitman, LS Jon Weeks

The battery of Piñeiro, Waitman and Weeks has been consistent throughout the summer, including a stellar performance from Piñeiro on Thursday. The only quibble is Piñeiro’s kickoff placement. Waitman could get tapped for that duty during the regular season, though Piñeiro handled all the kickoffs against the Raiders.
